video_script.anchor: What must each worker measure?
video_script.design: One idea: the same shape can be asked about in two different ways, along its edge and across its inside. It assumes nothing. There is no wrong idea to break in a hook. The anchor question appears only at the end, so there are no clears.
never_show: any length, number or symbol anywhere in the frame
the words perimeter and area
which job needs which measurement
maths_rules: The plot is a plain rectangle with no length, number or symbol written anywhere in the video.
Akshi's job is drawn as a teal line laid along the whole edge of the plot, and it never touches the inside.
Toshi's job is drawn as amber square tiles filling the whole inside of the plot, and they never cross the edge.
Both jobs sit on the same plot at the same size, so the child sees one shape and two jobs.
No answer is given: the video stops on the open question.
video_script.substitution: The two jobs ask two different questions about the same shape, so each worker measures something different.

media.teaching_notes: Stop 1 (the last beat, on the plot with the fence and the tiles): Akshi has to fence the edge and Toshi has to tile the inside. What do you think each of them has to measure before they can start? Answer: no right answer, this is a prediction. Also accept: anything at all, including the edge, the inside, the length, the size, I do not know. If stuck: Look at the plot. Akshi's job is along the edge. Toshi's job is inside the edge. If wrong: none, a hook question cannot be wrong; repeat the child's idea back warmly and say let us find out if that is what they need. Nothing is taught here: the words perimeter and area are not said, and they arrive in the next topic.

content.text:
A plot of land lies empty, marked out with pegs and string. Seen from above, it is a plain rectangle.
Akshi has a job on this plot. She must put a fence along its whole edge, starting at one corner and walking until she is back where she began.
Toshi has a job on the same plot. The ground inside the edge must be covered with square tiles, row after row, until no ground is left.
So there are two jobs on one shape. One job runs along the edge and the other fills the inside.
Before either of them can start, each must measure something. What do you think Akshi has to measure, and what does Toshi have to measure?

media.description: Three identical rectangles are displayed across two levels. On the upper left, a rectangle has a thick teal boundary and a white interior, with a dotted horizontal arrow pointing right above its top edge; below it, a card reads "Perimeter: the walk around the edge.". A vertical dashed line separates the upper shapes, labeled "different questions" reading upward. On the upper right, the rectangle has an amber fill and a thin grey boundary, above a card reading "Area: the covering inside.". Centered below, the rectangle combines both features with a thick teal boundary and amber fill, labeled "One shape. Two things to measure.".
media.teaching_notes: Show it after the child has traced the edge of a notebook with a finger. Ask which drawing is the walk and which is the covering. Return to it whenever a child adds when they should multiply, or the reverse.

media.generation_prompt:
MATHEMATICAL IMAGE REQUIREMENT
Teaching purpose: Make it obvious that the perimeter lives on the edge and the area lives inside: the same rectangle is shown with only its boundary in teal, then with only its inside in amber, then with both.

Composition: Flat, friendly educational illustration for a middle-school maths lesson: plain white background, thin uniform dark outlines (#2B2B2B), flat fills with no shading and no gradients, clean sans-serif labels in plain classroom English a child can read aloud. Colour-blind-safe colours: teal #0072B2 for the boundary or perimeter, drawn on the boundary line, amber #E69F00 for the enclosed region or area, drawn filling the inside, green #009E73 for a correct or matched case, reddish purple #CC79A7 for the piece being asked about, grey #6B7280 for construction lines and grids, muted red #D55E00 only for a wrong or impossible case, never as decoration. 16:9 landscape, 1456 by 816 pixels. Two large panels side by side on a white background, separated by a vertical dashed grey line, and a wide bottom strip beneath them. Flat illustration, thin dark outlines, flat fills. The rectangle is the same size and position in all three drawings.

Exact mathematical structure:
- Exactly 3 drawings of the same rectangle, at the same size, with no number or letter on any side.
- In the left panel only the boundary is coloured, thick and teal, and the inside is white.
- In the right panel only the inside is coloured, amber, and the boundary is thin and grey.
- In the bottom strip the edge is teal and the inside is amber together.
- A vertical dashed grey line separates the left and right panels, and the words different questions run along it, turned to read upwards.

Panels, left to right:
- Left panel The rectangle with its boundary drawn thick in teal and its inside left white, and a small dotted arrow along the top edge showing the direction of the walk. Below it the words: Perimeter: the walk around the edge.
- Right panel The same rectangle with its inside filled amber and its boundary thin and grey. Below it the words: Area: the covering inside.
- Bottom strip The same rectangle drawn a third time with a thick teal edge and an amber inside together. Beneath it the words: One shape. Two things to measure.

Visible text:
- Perimeter: the walk around the edge.
- Area: the covering inside.
- different questions
- One shape. Two things to measure.

Critical rejection conditions:
- any number, length, letter or unit written anywhere in the picture
- the boundary drawn filled or the inside drawn as a line: the edge is always teal and the inside is always amber
- the three rectangles drawn at different sizes or with different proportions
- any muted red or green, because nothing is wrong or matched here
- any text beyond the listed visible text, or any listed text misspelled or altered
- any board name, publisher name, book title, page number or curriculum branding anywhere in the frame
- a right angle drawn visibly different from 90 degrees, or sides that are shown equal but drawn visibly unequal
- perimeter drawn as a filled region or area drawn as a line: the boundary is always teal on the edge, the inside is always amber

Student takeaway: The perimeter is the walk along the edge; the area is the covering inside; they are two different questions about one shape.

video_script.anchor: What is the perimeter of this rectangle?
video_script.design: One idea: a rectangle has two of each side, so its walk is two lengths and two breadths. It assumes the child knows what the edge of a shape is. The wrong idea is some students's: add only the length and the breadth. The anchor question stays up all video; one clear, at the part boundary before the recap.
never_show: the sum twelve plus eight plus twelve plus eight completed before the idea part
the answer to the your-turn question: twenty-eight centimetres
video_script.wrong_move: some students adds only the length and the breadth, twelve plus eight, and gets twenty; the walk that traces the edge then crosses four sides and uses all of them.
maths_rules: The rectangle is called ABCD. Side AB is the top at 12 cm and side BC is the right side at 8 cm. The bottom side and the left side carry no number until the child has answered.
Opposite sides of a rectangle are equal, so the bottom is 12 cm and the left side is 8 cm.
The walk is 12 + 8 + 12 + 8 = 40 cm, drawn as a teal line traced round the edge, never as a filled region.
some students's slip is 12 + 8 = 20 cm, which uses only two of the four sides; the walk then crosses all four sides and 20 fails.
The two twelves slide together to make 2 x 12 and the two eights make 2 x 8, which collapse to 2 x (12 + 8) = 2 x 20 = 40 cm.
your turn: a rectangle with length 9 cm and breadth 5 cm, so the perimeter is 2 x (9 + 5) = 28 cm, never shown.
video_script.payoff_line: A rectangle has two of each side

final_answer.spoken: forty centimetres

video_script.substitution: A rectangle has two of each side, so the walk round it is two lengths plus two breadths, which is two times the length plus the breadth.

media.teaching_notes: Stop 1 (after the book question): Only two sides of the rectangle have numbers. How long is the bottom side? Answer: 12 cm. Also accept: 12, twelve, the same as the top, 12 centimetres. If stuck: Look at the top side and the bottom side. What is true about opposite sides of a rectangle? If wrong (8): The bottom is opposite the top, not opposite the eight centimetre side. Opposite sides of a rectangle match. Stop 2 (after the slip): Add up the whole walk, twelve, eight, twelve and eight. What is the perimeter? Answer: 40 cm. Also accept: 40, forty, 40 centimetres. If stuck: Add the two twelves first, which makes twenty-four. Now add the two eights. If wrong (20): That is twelve plus eight, only two sides. The walk goes all the way round, so it crosses four sides. Stop 3 (the your-turn question, at the end): A rectangle has a length of nine centimetres and a breadth of five centimetres. What is its perimeter? Answer: 28 cm. Also accept: 28, twenty-eight, 28 centimetres. If stuck: Two nines and two fives, or two times nine plus five. If wrong (14): That is nine plus five, only half the walk. Double it. Watch for M2: a child who gives twenty has added only the length and the breadth.

video_script.design: One idea: a square's walk is four times a side because its sides match, but a triangle's sides need not match, so its walk is the sides added. maths_rules: The photo frame is a square with every side 1 m. The tape runs along all four sides as a teal line, never as a filled region.
1 + 1 + 1 + 1 = 4 m, which rewrites as 4 × 1 = 4 m, because all four sides of a square are equal.
The triangle has sides of 4 cm, 5 cm and 7 cm, drawn clearly different in length, and no side is labelled with a total.
some students's slip is 5 × 3 = 15 cm, which treats the three sides as if they matched; they do not, so the sides are added: 4 + 5 + 7 = 16 cm.
Usha's square park has sides of 75 m: one round is 4 × 75 = 300 m and three rounds are 3 × 300 = 900 m.
your turn: a square park with sides of 60 m walked twice, so one round is 4 × 60 = 240 m and two rounds are 480 m, never shown.

final_answer.spoken: sixteen centimetres

video_script.substitution: A square has four equal sides, so its walk is four times a side; a triangle's sides can differ, so its walk is the three sides added.

media.teaching_notes: Stop 1 (the book question, the last beat of the hook): Each side of the frame is one metre. How much tape does Debojeet need altogether? Answer: 4 m. Also accept: 4, four, 4 metres, 4 m. If stuck: Count the sides of a square. How many are there, and how long is each? If wrong (1): That is one side only. The tape has to go all the way round, so think how many sides it crosses. Stop 2 (after the slip): The triangle's sides are 4, 5 and 7 centimetres. What is its perimeter? Answer: 16 cm. Also accept: 16, sixteen, 16 cm, add them up. If stuck: Add the three sides one after another. If wrong (15, or yes it can be multiplied): That trick works for a square because its sides are equal. Look at 4, 5 and 7: are those equal? Stop 3 (the your-turn question, at the end): A square park has sides of 60 metres and Charan walks two rounds of it. How far does Charan walk altogether? Answer: 480 m. Also accept: 480, four hundred eighty, 480 metres. If stuck: Find one round first, then think about two rounds. If wrong (240): That is one round only. Charan walks two rounds. content.text: Walk once all the way round a shape, starting and stopping at the same corner. Which part of the shape have you walked along: the edge or the inside?
content.prompt: Walk once all the way round a shape, starting and stopping at the same corner. Which part of the shape have you walked along: the edge or the inside?
content.publication_text: Walk once all the way round a shape, starting and stopping at the same corner. Which part of the shape have you walked along: the edge or the inside?

content.text:
Trace the edge of your own book with a finger. Start at one corner, go all the way round, and stop at the same corner.
That finger journey follows the boundary of the shape. The distance along the boundary, once all the way round, is called the perimeter.
A closed shape made only of straight sides is called a polygon. Its perimeter is the sum of the lengths of all its sides.
Look at the picture. One rectangle is drawn three times. In one drawing only the edge is teal: that is the walk. In another only the inside is amber: that is the covering. They are two different questions about one shape.

content.text: A rectangle shows its length on one side and its breadth on another. Do you think those two numbers are enough to find the walk all the way round?
content.prompt: A rectangle shows its length on one side and its breadth on another. Do you think those two numbers are enough to find the walk all the way round?
content.publication_text: A rectangle shows its length on one side and its breadth on another. Do you think those two numbers are enough to find the walk all the way round?

content.text:
A rectangle has four sides. Opposite sides are always equal, so the bottom matches the top and the left side matches the right side.
That means a rectangle has two lengths and two breadths. Walk once round the edge and you cross all four.
Add the four sides: length, breadth, length, breadth. The two lengths can be added together and so can the two breadths, so the walk is two lots of length plus breadth.
The perimeter of a rectangle is two times the length plus the breadth. The two is there because a rectangle has two of each side.

content.text:
A rectangle ABCD has a length of 12 cm and a breadth of 8 cm. What is its perimeter, and why does the rule double a sum?
1. Opposite sides of a rectangle are equal, so AB = CD = 12 cm and BC = DA = 8 cm.
2. Walk once round the edge: AB + BC + CD + DA = 12 + 8 + 12 + 8 = 40 cm.
3. Two twelves and two eights make 2 × 12 + 2 × 8, which is 2 × (12 + 8).
4. So the perimeter is 2 × (12 + 8) = 2 × 20 = 40 cm.
Answer: 40 cm, which is 2 × (12 + 8): a rectangle has two of each side.

content.text: A square has four equal sides, and a triangle can have three different sides. Which of the two do you think has a shortcut for its walk?

content.text:
All four sides of a square are the same length. So instead of adding the same number four times, we can multiply one side by four.
The perimeter of a square is four times the length of one side.
The three sides of a triangle can all be different. Then there is no shortcut, and the perimeter is the three sides added.
A rectangle's perimeter is two times the length plus the breadth, so the lace round a rectangular tablecloth is its perimeter.
When someone goes round a shape more than once, find the distance for one round first. Then multiply it by the number of rounds.

All four sides of a square are the same length. So instead of adding the same number four times, we can multiply one side by four.
The perimeter of a square is four times the length of one side.
The three sides of a triangle can all be different. Then there is no shortcut, and the perimeter is the three sides added.

Debojeet wants to put coloured tape all round a square photo frame whose sides are 1 m. How much tape does he need?

video_script.design: One idea: when the whole walk is known, take away the sides you know and share what is left. It assumes the child can find the perimeter of a rectangle and a square. The wrong idea is some students's: take away only one breadth. The anchor question stays up from the hook to the break; one clear, at the part boundary before the idea.

the answer to the your-turn question: eleven centimetres
video_script.wrong_move: some students takes away only one breadth of two from the fourteen and says twelve; the walk holds two breadths, so ten is left for the two lengths.
maths_rules: The rectangle has a breadth of 2 cm and a perimeter of 14 cm. The length carries a question mark and no number until the child has answered.
The walk is lifted off and laid flat as a teal string 14 cm long. Two pieces of 2 cm are marked off for the two breadths, which leaves 14 - 2 - 2 = 10 cm for the two lengths.
The 10 cm is shared between two equal lengths, so each length is 10 ÷ 2 = 5 cm.
some students's slip is 14 - 2 = 12 cm, which takes away only one breadth; the string holds two breadths.
The square has a perimeter of 20 cm and four equal sides, so each side is 20 ÷ 4 = 5 cm.
your turn: a rectangle with a walk of 30 cm and a breadth of 4 cm, so 30 - 4 - 4 = 22 cm, shared between two lengths gives 11 cm, never shown.

final_answer.spoken: the length is five centimetres and the side of the square is five centimetres

video_script.substitution: Take away the sides you know from the whole walk, then share what is left between the sides that are missing.

media.teaching_notes: Stop 1 (the book question, the last beat of the hook): A rectangle has a breadth of 2 centimetres and a walk of 14 centimetres. How long is the length of this rectangle? Answer: 5 cm. Also accept: 5, five, 5 cm, 5 centimetres. If stuck: Lay the walk flat as a string. How much of it do the two breadths use? If wrong (12): You took away one breadth. There are two breadths in the walk, so two lots of two are used. If wrong (10): Ten is what is left for both lengths together. How long is each one? Stop 2 (after the slip): Two pieces of two centimetres are used. How much string is left for the two lengths? Answer: 10 cm. Also accept: 10, ten, 10 cm. If stuck: Start with 14, take away 2, then take away 2 again. If wrong (12): You took away one 2. There are two short sides, so two 2s have gone. Stop 3 (the your-turn question, at the end): A rectangle has a walk of 30 centimetres and a breadth of 4 centimetres. How long is its length? Answer: 11 cm. Also accept: 11, eleven, 11 cm. If stuck: Take away the two breadths from the walk, then share what is left between the two lengths. If wrong (22): Twenty-two is for both lengths together. Share it between the two. If wrong (26): You took away one breadth only. There are two breadths. Watch for M2: a child who takes away only one of the two equal sides has forgotten the walk crosses four sides. The square, perimeter 20 cm, is shown in the idea part with no stop, because it follows the same sharing idea.

media.teaching_notes: Stop 1 (the book question, the last beat of the hook): A wire bent into a rectangle 5 centimetres by 3 centimetres is straightened and bent into a square. How long is each side of the square? Answer: 4 cm. Also accept: 4, four, 4 cm, 4 centimetres. If stuck: Add up the four sides of the rectangle to find how much wire there is. content.text: The whole walk round a shape is known, and some of its sides are known, but one side is missing. How could you find that side?
content.prompt: The whole walk round a shape is known, and some of its sides are known, but one side is missing. How could you find that side?
content.publication_text: The whole walk round a shape is known, and some of its sides are known, but one side is missing. How could you find that side?

content.text:
Sometimes the whole walk is known and a side is missing. Then the perimeter rule runs backwards.
Lay the walk flat as a string. Take away the pieces for the sides you know. What is left must make the sides that are missing.
A rectangle has two lengths and two breadths. Take away each known side twice, then share what is left between the two sides that are missing.
A square has four equal sides, so share the whole walk between four.
A triangle has three sides. Add the two known sides, then take that away from the whole walk.

content.text: A piece of wire is bent into a rectangle, then straightened and bent into a square. Do you think the square needs more wire, less wire or the same wire?
content.prompt: A piece of wire is bent into a rectangle, then straightened and bent into a square. Do you think the square needs more wire, less wire or the same wire?
content.publication_text: A piece of wire is bent into a rectangle, then straightened and bent into a square. Do you think the square needs more wire, less wire or the same wire?

content.text:
A wire has a fixed length. Bend it into a rectangle, straighten it, then bend it into a square: nothing is cut off, so its length does not change.
The wire is the perimeter of whatever shape it makes. So every shape bent from the same wire has the same perimeter, even though the shapes look different.
When all the sides of a shape are equal, share the wire equally. Divide the length of the wire by the number of sides to find one side.
A fence or a rope that goes round a field is a perimeter too. Find one round first. For a cost, multiply the length of the fence by the price of one metre. For several rounds, multiply one round by the number of rounds.

content.question_tex: Usha takes three rounds of a square park whose sides are $75\text{ m}$. How far does she travel?
content.publication_text: Usha takes three rounds of a square park whose sides are $75\text{ m}$. How far does she travel?

content.text:
$1$. The perimeter of the square park is $4 \times 75\text{ m} = 300\text{ m}$.
$2$. One round is $300\text{ m}$.
$3$. Three rounds are $3 \times 300\text{ m} = 900\text{ m}$.
Answer: $300\text{ m}$ in one round, $900\text{ m}$ in three rounds.

There are two lengths in the walk, so two threes are used up. Stop 2 (the hint, before the second try): Try the question again with the hint: how long is the breadth of this rectangle? Answer: 3 m. Also accept: 3, three, 3 m, three metres, 3 metres. If stuck: Twelve take away three, and take away three again. Then share what is left between the two breadths. If wrong (9): That takes away one length only. Take the second length away too. Stop 3 (the second question, in the idea part): A triangle has a perimeter of fifty-five centimetres, and two sides of twenty and fourteen centimetres. How long is the third side? Answer: 21 cm. Also accept: 21, twenty-one, 21 cm, twenty-one centimetres. If stuck: Add twenty and fourteen first. Then take that away from fifty-five. If wrong (35): Check the adding: twenty and fourteen make thirty-four, not twenty. Watch for M2: a child who gives nine has taken away only one of the two lengths. Honesty note: the printed solution writes the breadth as three centimetres; the question is in metres, so the video says three metres.

video_script.design: One idea: a fence or rope round a field is its perimeter; find one round first, then multiply by the price or by the number of rounds. It assumes the child can find the perimeter of a rectangle. The wrong idea is some students's: add only one length and one breadth. The anchor question stays up from the hook to the break; one clear, at the part boundary before the idea.

maths_rules: The park is a rectangle 150 m long and 120 m wide. The fence is a teal line right round its edge, never a filled region.
The fence costs Rs 40 for every metre. The cost is the length of the fence times the price of one metre.
some students's slip is 150 + 120 = 270 m, which is one length and one breadth only; the fence passes all four sides.
The fence is 2 × (150 + 120) = 2 × 270 = 540 m, and the cost is 540 × 40 = 21600 rupees.
The field is 230 m long and 160 m wide: one round is 2 × (230 + 160) = 2 × 390 = 780 m and three rounds need 3 × 780 = 2340 m of rope.
your turn: a field 80 m long and 45 m wide with two rounds of rope, so one round is 2 × (80 + 45) = 250 m and two rounds need 500 m, never shown.

content.text: $(a)$: The perimeter of a rectangle is $14\text{ cm}$ and its breadth is $2\text{ cm}$. Find its length. $(b)$: The perimeter of a square is $20\text{ cm}$. Find its side.
content.question: (a) The perimeter of a rectangle is 14 cm and its breadth is 2 cm. Find its length. (b) The perimeter of a square is 20 cm. Find its side.
content.book_number: Which side is missing in the 14 cm rectangle and the 20 cm square?
content.question_tex: $(a)$: The perimeter of a rectangle is $14\text{ cm}$ and its breadth is $2\text{ cm}$. Find its length. $(b)$: The perimeter of a square is $20\text{ cm}$. Find its side.
content.publication_text: $(a)$: The perimeter of a rectangle is $14\text{ cm}$ and its breadth is $2\text{ cm}$. Find its length. $(b)$: The perimeter of a square is $20\text{ cm}$. Find its side.

content.text:
$1$. $(a)$: Lay the walk flat as a string $14\text{ cm}$ long. The two breadths use $2\text{ cm} + 2\text{ cm} = 4\text{ cm}$.
$2$. $14\text{ cm} - 4\text{ cm} = 10\text{ cm}$ is left for the two lengths.
$3$. The two lengths are equal, so each is $10 \div 2 = 5\text{ cm}$.
$4$. $(b)$: A square has four equal sides, so each side is $20 \div 4 = 5\text{ cm}$.
Answer: $(a)$: length $5\text{ cm}$, $(b)$: side $5\text{ cm}$.

(b) A square has four equal sides, so each side is 20 ÷ 4 = 5 cm.

$3$. Check: $20 + 14 + 21 = 55\text{ cm}$.

content.text: A rectangle with sides of $5\text{ cm}$ and $3\text{ cm}$ is made from a piece of wire. The wire is straightened and then bent into a square. Find the side of the square.

content.book_number: What is the side of the square bent from the wire?
content.question_tex: A rectangle with sides of $5\text{ cm}$ and $3\text{ cm}$ is made from a piece of wire. The wire is straightened and then bent into a square. Find the side of the square.
content.publication_text: A rectangle with sides of $5\text{ cm}$ and $3\text{ cm}$ is made from a piece of wire. The wire is straightened and then bent into a square. Find the side of the square.

content.text:
$1$. The wire is the perimeter of the rectangle: $2 \times (5 + 3) = 2 \times 8 = 16\text{ cm}$.
$2$. Straightening and bending the wire does not change its length, so the square also has a perimeter of $16\text{ cm}$.
$3$. A square has four equal sides, so each side is $16 \div 4 = 4\text{ cm}$.
Answer: Side $4\text{ cm}$.

$1$. The whole string is used each time, so the perimeter is $36\text{ cm}$.

$3$. $(b)$: A triangle with equal sides has three: $36 \div 3 = 12\text{ cm}$.
$4$. $(c)$: A hexagon has six equal sides: $36 \div 6 = 6\text{ cm}$.
Answer: $9\text{ cm}$, $12\text{ cm}$ and $6\text{ cm}$.

content.text: What would be the cost of fencing a rectangular park whose length is $150\text{ m}$ and breadth is $120\text{ m}$, if the fence costs Rs $40$ for every metre?
content.question: What would be the cost of fencing a rectangular park whose length is 150 m and breadth is 120 m, if the fence costs Rs 40 for every metre?
content.book_number: What does it cost to fence the park?
content.question_tex: What would be the cost of fencing a rectangular park whose length is $150\text{ m}$ and breadth is $120\text{ m}$, if the fence costs Rs $40$ for every metre?
content.publication_text: What would be the cost of fencing a rectangular park whose length is $150\text{ m}$ and breadth is $120\text{ m}$, if the fence costs Rs $40$ for every metre?

content.text:
$1$. The fence goes all the way round the park, so its length is the perimeter: $2 \times (150 + 120) = 2 \times 270 = 540\text{ m}$.
$2$. Each metre of fence costs Rs $40$, so the cost is $540 \times 40 = 21600$ rupees.
$3$. The cost is Rs $21,600$.
Answer: $540\text{ m}$ of fence, so Rs $21,600$.

content.text:
$1$. One round of rope is the perimeter of the field: $2 \times (230 + 160) = 2 \times 390 = 780\text{ m}$.
$2$. Three rounds need $3 \times 780 = 2340\text{ m}$ of rope.
$3$. The total length of rope is $2,340\text{ m}$.
Answer: $780\text{ m}$ for one round, so $2,340\text{ m}$ of rope.

maths_rules: Akshi's outer track is a rectangle 70 m long and 40 m wide. Toshi's inner track is a rectangle 60 m long and 30 m wide, drawn inside the outer one. The rounds counters show only the number of rounds, 5 and 7, never a distance, until the idea part.
One round of the outer track is 2 × (70 + 40) = 220 m, drawn as a teal line traced once round the edge. Five rounds are five copies of 220 stacked in a column: 220 + 220 + 220 + 220 + 220 = 1100 m.
One round of the inner track is 2 × (60 + 30) = 180 m. Seven copies of 180 stack to 7 × 180 = 1260 m.

media.teaching_notes: Folded hook: Who Ran Further? opens this video. Its situation is the first beat of the hook part and its one prediction question is the first stop. Stop 1 (the hook, after the situation): Who do you think ran further, Akshi with five big rounds or Toshi with seven smaller ones? Answer: no right answer, this is a prediction. Also accept: anything at all, including Akshi, Toshi, the same, I cannot tell yet. If stuck: Just pick one. We will find out in a minute. If wrong (anything): none, a prediction cannot be wrong; say let us test it and play on. Stop 2 (after the slip): How long is one round of Akshi's track? Answer: 220 m. Also accept: 220, two hundred twenty, 220 metres. If stuck: Seventy plus forty is one length and one breadth. A round has two of each. If wrong (110): That is one length and one breadth. A round goes all the way round, so it crosses four sides. Stop 3 (Toshi's track, in the idea part): How long is one round of Toshi's track? Answer: 180 m. Also accept: 180, one hundred eighty, 180 metres. If stuck: Sixty plus thirty is ninety. Now double it. If wrong (90): That is only halfway round. Double it for the full round. Stop 4 (the your-turn question, at the end): A track is forty-five metres long and fifteen metres wide. A runner runs four rounds. How far does she run? Answer: 480 m. Also accept: 480, four hundred eighty, 480 metres. If stuck: Find one round first, two times forty-five plus fifteen. Then take four of them. If wrong (120): That is one round. She ran four rounds, so repeat it. Watch for M2: a child who gives one hundred ten has added only one length and one breadth.

video_script.anchor: Where is she now?
video_script.design: One idea: a distance on a loop is whole rounds plus a leftover, and the leftover shows where she stands. It assumes the child can find one round of a rectangle. maths_rules: Akshi's track is a rectangle 70 m long and 40 m wide, so one round is 220 m. The start is marked on the track. A distance counter climbs and, each time it passes a multiple of 220, a round counter ticks and the marker flashes through the start.
250 m: one round uses 220, and 250 - 220 = 30, so Akshi is 30 m past the start, drawn as a short teal arc from the start.
500 m: two rounds are 2 × 220 = 440, and 500 - 440 = 60, so two full rounds and 60 m past the start. Three rounds would be 660, which is more than 500.
1000 m: four rounds are 4 × 220 = 880, and 1000 - 880 = 120, so four full rounds and 120 m past the start.
some students's slip is that 250 m run means 250 m along the track, which cannot be true on a track only 220 m round.
your turn: a track 190 m round and 700 m run. Three rounds are 3 × 190 = 570, and 700 - 570 = 130 m past the start, never shown.

media.teaching_notes: Stop 1 (the hook, after the setting): One round of the track is two hundred twenty metres and Akshi has run two hundred fifty metres. How far past the start is she? Answer: 30 m. Also accept: 30, thirty, 30 metres, 30 metres past the start. If stuck: She has finished one whole round. Take two hundred twenty away from two hundred fifty. If wrong (250): She cannot be two hundred fifty metres along a track that is only two hundred twenty metres round. She has gone past the start once. Stop 2 (after the slip): After five hundred metres, how many full rounds has she finished? Answer: 2. Also accept: 2, two, two rounds, two full rounds. If stuck: How many two hundred twenties fit inside five hundred? If wrong (3): Three rounds would be six hundred sixty, which is more than five hundred. Try two. Stop 3 (the your-turn question, at the end): A track is one hundred ninety metres round and a runner has run seven hundred metres. How far past the start is she? Answer: 130 m. Also accept: 130, one hundred thirty, 130 metres past the start. If stuck: Find how many whole rounds of one hundred ninety fit inside seven hundred, and take them away. If wrong (510): That takes away only one round of one hundred ninety. More whole rounds fit inside seven hundred, so take away all of them.

content.text: Akshi ran five rounds of a big track and Toshi ran seven rounds of a smaller one. Who do you think ran further? Nobody is marking this guess.
content.prompt: Akshi ran five rounds of a big track and Toshi ran seven rounds of a smaller one. Who do you think ran further? Nobody is marking this guess.
content.publication_text: Akshi ran five rounds of a big track and Toshi ran seven rounds of a smaller one. Who do you think ran further? Nobody is marking this guess.

content.text:
A runner who goes round a track once covers the whole edge of the track. For a rectangle that is two lengths and two breadths.
The distance for several rounds is one round, repeated. Five rounds means five copies of the same distance, and five copies added together is the same as five times one round.
So there are always two steps. First find one round. Then multiply it by the number of rounds.
A longer track does not always mean a longer run. A runner on a smaller track can go further by running more rounds, so the two totals must be worked out and compared.

content.text:
A track is a loop. When the distance run reaches one whole round, the runner is back at the start and a new round begins.
To find where a runner stands, take away whole rounds first. Whatever is left over is how far she is past the start.
For 250 metres on a track of 220 metres a round, one whole round uses 220, and 250 - 220 leaves 30. She is 30 metres past the start.
To count full rounds, see how many whole rounds fit inside the distance. The leftover is always less than one round.

media.teaching_notes: Stop 1 (the hook, after the setting): One round of Toshi's track is one hundred eighty metres and she has run two hundred fifty metres. How far past the start is she? Answer: 70 m. Also accept: 70, seventy, 70 metres, 70 metres past the start. If stuck: Take away one whole round of one hundred eighty from two hundred fifty. If wrong (250): She cannot be two hundred fifty metres along a track that is only one hundred eighty metres round. Stop 2 (the hint, before the second try): Try the question again with the hint: how far past the start is Toshi after two hundred fifty metres? Answer: 70 m. Also accept: 70, seventy, 70 metres, 70 metres past the start. If stuck: Each time the run passes one hundred eighty metres she is back at the start. Take one hundred eighty away from two hundred fifty, and see what is left. If wrong (180): That is the whole round. The leftover is what remains after the round is taken away. Stop 3 (the last stop, in the idea part): Toshi has run a thousand metres. How many full rounds has she finished? Answer: 5. Also accept: 5, five, five rounds, five full rounds. If stuck: How many one hundred eighties fit inside a thousand? If wrong (6): Six rounds would be one thousand eighty, which is more than a thousand. Try five. concepts.concept_name: Round and Round the Track: Q1

content.text:
$1$. One round is the whole edge of the track: $2 \times (70 + 40) = 2 \times 110 = 220\text{ m}$.
$2$. Five rounds are five copies of $220\text{ m}$: $220 + 220 + 220 + 220 + 220 = 1100\text{ m}$.
$3$. That is the same as $5 \times 220 = 1100\text{ m}$.
Answer: Akshi ran $1,100\text{ m}$: $220\text{ m}$ a round, so five rounds make $1,100\text{ m}$.

concepts.concept_name: Round and Round the Track: Q5

content.text:
{{DIAGRAM:M1.S7.T7.C39.IMG1}}
$1$. Walk backwards from the flag, against the arrows. The flag is in the middle of a side, so the first corner is half a side back.
$2$. Inner track: half of $100$ is $50\text{ m}$ to the corner, then three whole sides of $100\text{ m}$: $50 + 100 + 100 + 100 = 350\text{ m}$. For runner $A$, the start is at a corner.
$3$. Outer track: half of $150$ is $75\text{ m}$ to the corner, then a whole side of $150\text{ m}$, which makes $225\text{ m}$ so far. $350 - 225 = 125\text{ m}$ more along the next side: $75 + 150 + 125 = 350\text{ m}$. $B$ starts on the third side counted back from the flag, $125\text{ m}$ from the corner.
Answer: $A$ is $350\text{ m}$ back from the flag on the inner track: $100 + 100 + 100 + 50$. $B$ is $350\text{ m}$ back on the outer track: $125 + 150 + 75$.

- In the middle panel both lengths start at the same left-hand end, and the slanted one extends visibly further to the right than the straight one.

- The muted red bracket marks only the extra length of the slanted line, where the straight length does not match it.

Panels, left to right:
- Left panel A single unit square on a small dot grid. Its straight side is drawn thick in teal and its slanted corner to corner line is drawn thick in reddish purple, both starting from the same corner so they share an origin.
- Middle panel The two lengths lifted off the square and laid flat one above the other, both starting from the same left-hand end. The reddish purple one is visibly longer. The extra bit at its right end is marked with a muted red bracket labelled: the extra.
- Right panel A right-angled triangle on a dot grid with two straight sides of three units each, drawn teal, and one slanted side of three diagonal units, drawn reddish purple. Beneath it the words: 6s + 3d.

Visible text:
- s
- d
- the extra
- 6s + 3d
- One straight unit is called s. One slanted unit is called d. d is longer, so we never mix them.

Critical rejection conditions:
- the slanted line drawn the same length as the straight side, or shorter
- the two lengths in the middle panel starting from different left-hand ends, so the comparison cannot be seen
- the triangle drawn with a different number of straight or slanted units from three and three
- the muted red bracket used on anything except the extra length, because it marks a length that does not match
- any text beyond the listed visible text, or any listed text misspelled or altered
- any board name, publisher name, book title, page number or curriculum branding anywhere in the frame
- a right angle drawn visibly different from 90 degrees, or sides that are shown equal but drawn visibly unequal
- perimeter drawn as a filled region or area drawn as a line: the boundary is always teal on the edge, the inside is always amber

Student takeaway: A slanted unit is longer than a straight unit, so a dot grid walk is written in two piles, s and d, and the two are never mixed.

media.teaching_notes: Stop 1 (the hook, after the setting): Look at an edge that goes straight across and an edge that slants. Do you think they are the same length? Answer: No. Also accept: no, the slanted one is longer, they are different, not the same. If stuck: Imagine walking straight across a square and then walking corner to corner. Which walk is longer? If wrong (yes): Have a closer look. We are about to lay one on top of the other and see. Stop 2 (after the slip): Is the real walk less than nine units, exactly nine, or more than nine? Answer: more than nine. Also accept: more, more than 9, bigger, longer. If stuck: Three of the nine edges are longer than a straight unit. So does the total go up or down? If wrong (less): The slanted edges are longer, not shorter, so the total has to be more, not less. Stop 3 (the your-turn question, at the end): A triangle on a dot grid has two straight sides of two units each and one slanted side of two diagonal units. Write its perimeter in s and d. Answer: 4s + 2d. Also accept: four s and two d, 4 straight and 2 diagonal, 4s plus 2d. If stuck: Count the straight units in one pile and the diagonal units in the other pile. If wrong (6): That adds a straight unit to a diagonal unit. They are different lengths, so keep two piles. Watch for M3: a child who says nine has counted a slanted edge as one straight unit.

maths_rules: The equilateral triangle ABC has all three sides marked equal, with no numbers. Its perimeter is AB + BC + AC = AB + AB + AB = 3 × AB.
A square is drawn with four equal sides, and its perimeter is 4 × a side.
A regular polygon has all sides equal and all angles equal. A square and an equilateral triangle are both regular, and that is what they have in common.
A regular pentagon has 5 equal sides and a regular hexagon has 6 equal sides. The hexagon has sides of 5 cm.
some students's slip is 6 + 5 = 11 cm, which adds the number of sides to the side length instead of repeating the side.
A regular hexagon with six sides of 5 cm: 5 + 5 + 5 + 5 + 5 + 5 = 30 cm, which is 6 × 5 = 30 cm.

If stuck: How many sides does a triangle have? If wrong (the sides added, 12): Adding the sides is right, but three equal sides are three copies of one side, so you can multiply. Stop 2 (after the slip): A regular hexagon has six equal sides of five centimetres. What is its perimeter? Answer: 30 cm. Also accept: 30, thirty, 30 centimetres. If stuck: Write five six times and add, or take six lots of five. If wrong (11): That looks like adding six and five. We want six lots of five. Stop 3 (the your-turn question, at the end): A regular pentagon has five equal sides of twelve centimetres. What is its perimeter? Answer: 60 cm. Also accept: 60, sixty, 60 centimetres. If stuck: How many sides does a pentagon have? Take that many lots of twelve. If wrong (17): That adds five and twelve. We want five lots of twelve. Book note: the book names the square, the equilateral triangle and the regular pentagon, and asks the child to find other regular shapes. content.text:
On a dot grid, a unit that goes straight across or straight up and down is called a straight unit. The book draws these in red and writes s for one of them.
A unit that slants from one dot to a dot in the next row and the next column is called a diagonal unit. The book draws these in blue and writes d for one of them.
Lay one straight unit along one diagonal unit and the straight unit falls short. A diagonal unit is longer, so the two can never be counted as the same kind of unit.
So a perimeter on a dot grid is written in two piles. The book's triangle has six straight units and three diagonal units, which is written 6s + 3d. Its walk is more than nine units, because three of the nine edges are longer than a straight unit.

content.text:
A triangle with all three sides equal is called an equilateral triangle. Its perimeter is AB + BC + AC, and since the three sides are the same, that is AB + AB + AB.
Three copies of one side make three times that side. So the perimeter of an equilateral triangle is 3 × the length of a side.
A closed figure with all sides equal and all angles equal is called a regular polygon. A square is one, and so is an equilateral triangle. That is what the two share.
A regular pentagon has five equal sides and a regular hexagon has six. The same idea works every time: the perimeter of a regular polygon is the number of sides × the length of one side.

content.text:
Find the perimeter of an equilateral triangle ABC in terms of the length of one side.
1. The perimeter of any triangle is the sum of its three sides: AB + BC + AC.
2. All three sides are equal, so AB + BC + AC = AB + AB + AB.
3. Three copies of AB make 3 × AB.
Answer: 3 × the length of a side.

content.text:
What is a similarity between a square and an equilateral triangle?
1. A square has four equal sides and four equal angles.
2. An equilateral triangle has three equal sides and three equal angles.
3. Both have all sides equal and all angles equal, so both are regular polygons. That is why both perimeters are the number of sides × one side.
Answer: Both are regular: all sides equal and all angles equal, so both use the number of sides × one side.

media.teaching_notes: Stop 1 (the hook, after the setting): Look at the first shape. Count one unit for every gap between two dots. How many go straight, and how many slant? Answer: 8 straight and 2 slanted. Also accept: 8 and 2, 8s + 2d, eight straight and two slanted. If stuck: Go round the shape once. Every time the line goes flat or upright it is a straight one. Every time it slants it is a slanted one. If wrong (10): Ten is the number of units altogether. The two kinds are different lengths, so they stay in two separate piles. Stop 2 (the hint, before the second try): How many straight units and how many diagonal units are there in the first shape, counting one for every gap between two dots? Answer: eight straight units and two diagonal units. Also accept: 8 and 2, eight and two, 8s + 2d. If stuck: Start at the top left corner and count the units along the top, then go round, keeping two tallies. If wrong (10): That adds the two piles. Keep a tally for straight units and a separate tally for diagonal units. Watch for M3: a child who adds the two piles has treated a diagonal unit as a straight unit.

content.text:
$1$. Count the edges: six go straight across or straight up and down, and three slant.
$2$. Lay one straight unit on one slanted unit. It falls short, so a slanted unit is longer than a straight unit.
$3$. So the nine edges are not nine equal units. The perimeter is $6$ straight units plus $3$ diagonal units, written $6s + 3d$.
$4$. Three of the nine edges are longer than one straight unit, so the perimeter is more than $9\text{ units}$. Toshi is right.
Answer: No, Akshi is not right. The perimeter is more than $9\text{ units}$, because a slanted unit is longer than a straight unit.

content.text:
{{DIAGRAM:M1.S9.T9.C46.IMG1}}
$1$. Go round each shape once. Count one unit for every gap between two dots along the edge. Count straight units and diagonal units in two separate piles.
$2$. The first shape: $3 + 1 + 1 + 3 = 8$ straight units and $2$ diagonal units, so $8s + 2d$.
$3$. The second shape: $1 + 2 + 1 = 4$ straight units and $6$ diagonal units, so $4s + 6d$.
$4$. The third shape: $1 + 3 + 1 + 2 + 3 + 2 = 12$ straight units and $6$ diagonal units, so $12s + 6d$.
$5$. The fourth shape: $1 + 3 + 1 + 4 + 1 + 3 + 1 + 4 = 18$ straight units and $6$ diagonal units, so $18s + 6d$.
Answer: The four dot grid figures written in straight and diagonal units: $8s + 2d$, $4s + 6d$, $12s + 6d$ and $18s + 6d$.

concepts.concept_name: Straight Units and Slanted Units: Q3

content.text:
$1$. A regular pentagon has $5$ equal sides, so its perimeter is $5 \times$ one side. A regular hexagon has $6$ equal sides, so its perimeter is $6 \times$ one side.
$2$. A regular hexagon with each side $5\text{ cm}$ has a perimeter of $6 \times 5 = 30\text{ cm}$.
$3$. The pattern is the same for every regular polygon: write one side as many times as there are sides.
Answer: The perimeter of any regular polygon: the number of sides $\times$ the length of a side.

video_script.anchor: What is the perimeter of the joined shape?
video_script.design: One idea: the edges where two pieces touch are inside the new shape, so take the join away twice. It assumes the child can find the perimeter of a rectangle. maths_rules: The chit is 6 cm tall and 4 cm wide. It is cut down the middle into two equal pieces, each 6 cm by 2 cm. Each piece has a perimeter of 6 + 2 + 6 + 2 = 16 cm.
The two pieces are put together end to end, along their 2 cm edges, to make a strip 12 cm by 2 cm. The two touching edges turn grey and sink inside the strip.
some students's slip is 16 + 16 = 32 cm, which forgets that the join disappears.
The strip: 16 + 16 - 2 - 2 = 28 cm. The join has two sides, one on each piece, so twice the join is taken away: 32 - 2 × 2 = 28 cm.
The rule: the perimeter of the joined shape is the two perimeters added, minus twice the length of the join.
To make 22 cm, the pieces touch along 5 cm of their long edges: 16 + 16 - 2 × 5 = 32 - 10 = 22 cm.
your turn: two pieces each with perimeter 20 cm, touching along 4 cm: 20 + 20 - 2 × 4 = 32 cm, never shown.

media.teaching_notes: Folded hook: The Same Paper opens this video. Its situation, the chit cut into two equal pieces and put together in different ways, is the first beat of the hook part, and its one prediction question is the first stop. Stop 1 (the hook, after the situation): Same two pieces every time. Do you think the distance round the edge stays the same, or changes? Answer: no right answer, this is a prediction. Also accept: anything at all, including the same, it changes, I cannot tell yet. If stuck: Just say what you think. We are about to find out. If wrong (anything): none, a prediction cannot be wrong; say let us find out and play on. Stop 2 (after the slip): Are the two touching edges still part of the walk round the strip? Answer: No. Also accept: no, they are inside now, they do not count, not any more. If stuck: Trace round the outside of the strip with your finger. Do you ever walk along those edges? If wrong (yes): Trace round the outside with your finger. Do you ever touch those touching edges? Stop 3 (the twenty-two question, in the idea part): The pieces touch along five centimetres of their long edges. How much boundary is lost altogether? Answer: 10 cm. Also accept: 10, ten, twice five, five twice. If stuck: Each piece loses the join. How many pieces are there? If wrong (5): Five is what one piece loses. Both pieces lose five, because the join has two sides. Stop 4 (the your-turn question, at the end): Two pieces each have a perimeter of twenty centimetres, and they touch along four centimetres. What is the perimeter of the new shape? Answer: 32 cm. Also accept: 32, thirty-two, 32 centimetres. If stuck: Add the two perimeters, then take away the join twice. If wrong (40): That is the two perimeters added, with nothing taken away. Take away twice the join. Watch for M5: a child who gives thirty-two for the strip has forgotten that the join disappears.

content.text:
A paper chit is 6 cm tall and 4 cm wide. It is cut down the middle into two equal pieces, and each piece is 6 cm by 2 cm. The walk round one piece is 6 + 2 + 6 + 2 = 16 cm.
When two pieces are joined, the edges that touch are hidden inside the new shape. Nobody walks along them, so they are no longer part of the boundary.
The join has two sides, one on each piece. So two lengths of the join are lost, and the rule is: the perimeter of the joined shape is the two perimeters added, minus twice the length of the join.
A longer join hides more edge, so the perimeter gets smaller. The paper is the same each time. Only the edge changes.

content.text:
The chit, 6 cm by 4 cm, is cut into two equal pieces. The pieces are joined end to end along their 2 cm edges. What is the perimeter of this long strip?
{{DIAGRAM:M1.S10.T10.C49.IMG1}}
1. Each piece is 6 cm by 2 cm, so each has a perimeter of 6 + 2 + 6 + 2 = 16 cm.
2. The two pieces touch along a 2 cm edge. That edge is lost from each piece, so 2 cm + 2 cm = 4 cm leaves the boundary.
3. 16 + 16 - 2 - 2 = 28 cm. The strip is 12 cm by 2 cm, and 2 × (12 + 2) = 28 cm agrees.
Answer: 28 cm

content.text:
{{DIAGRAM:M1.S11.T11.C52.IMG1}}
$1$. The pieces are the same, so the two perimeters added are $16 + 16 = 32\text{ cm}$ each time. Only the join changes.
$2$. The $L$ shape joins along $2\text{ cm}$: $32 - 2 \times 2 = 28\text{ cm}$. Its six sides are $8$, $6$, $2$, $4$, $6$ and $2\text{ cm}$, and $8 + 6 + 2 + 4 + 6 + 2 = 28$ agrees.
$3$. The $T$ shape also joins along $2\text{ cm}$: $32 - 2 \times 2 = 28\text{ cm}$.
$4$. The last arrangement joins along $3\text{ cm}$: $32 - 2 \times 3 = 26\text{ cm}$.
Answer: The other three arrangements of the two pieces: $28\text{ cm}$, $28\text{ cm}$ and $26\text{ cm}$ (derived from the rule: the two perimeters added, minus twice the join).

content.text:
{{DIAGRAM:M1.S11.T11.C54.IMG1}}
$1$. The two perimeters add to $16 + 16 = 32\text{ cm}$. We want $22\text{ cm}$, so $32 - 22 = 10\text{ cm}$ must be lost.
$2$. The lost length is twice the join, so the join is $10 \div 2 = 5\text{ cm}$.
$3$. Slide one piece along the other so that they touch along $5\text{ cm}$ of their long edges. Check: $16 + 16 - 2 \times 5 = 22\text{ cm}$.
Answer: Join them along $5\text{ cm}$: $16 + 16 - 2 \times 5 = 22$.

video_script.design: One idea: to find a leftover region, find the whole area and take away the part that is covered. It assumes the child can multiply a length by a width. maths_rules: The floor is 5 m long and 4 m wide, drawn from above as a grid of 20 amber squares, each 1 m by 1 m. Its area is 5 x 4 = 20 sq m.
The square carpet is 3 m on each side and covers 3 x 3 = 9 squares, so its area is 9 sq m. The covered squares dim but stay visible.
some students's slip is 20 + 9 = 29 sq m, which adds the carpet to the floor; the carpet hides floor and does not add any.
The floor not carpeted is 20 - 9 = 11 sq m, drawn as the squares still amber.
The land is 12 m long and 10 m wide, area 12 x 10 = 120 sq m. Each of the four square flower beds is 4 m on a side, area 4 x 4 = 16 sq m.
The four beds cover 4 x 16 = 64 sq m, so the land that remains is 120 - 64 = 56 sq m.
your turn: a floor 8 m by 6 m with a square carpet of side 2 m, so the floor not carpeted is 8 x 6 - 2 x 2 = 44 sq m, never shown.
video_script.payoff_line: Take away the part that is covered

final_answer.spoken: eleven square metres of the floor and fifty-six square metres of the land

media.teaching_notes: Stop 1 (after the book question): How many square metres of the floor are not covered by the carpet? Answer: 11 sq m. Also accept: 11, eleven, 11 square metres, eleven square metres. If stuck: How many squares does the floor have, and how many does the carpet hide? If wrong (29): Adding would make the floor bigger. The carpet covers part of the floor, so we take away. Stop 2 (after the slip): How many square metres of the floor are not covered? Answer: 11 sq m. Also accept: 11, eleven, 11 square metres. If stuck: The carpet hides some squares of the floor. How many squares are left showing? If wrong (29): That is the carpet added to the floor. The carpet hides some floor, it does not add any. Stop 3 (the second question, in the idea part): What is the area of one flower bed? Answer: 16 sq m. Also accept: 16, sixteen, 16 square metres. If stuck: Four metres one way and four metres the other. How many square metres fit in? If wrong (8): Eight is four plus four, which is a walk along two sides. For area we multiply. Stop 4 (the your-turn question, at the end): A floor is 8 m long and 6 m wide and a square carpet of side 2 m lies on it. How many square metres of the floor are not covered? Answer: 44 sq m. Also accept: 44, forty-four, 44 square metres. If stuck: Find the area of the floor, then the area of the carpet, then take the carpet away. If wrong (52): That adds the carpet to the floor. The carpet hides floor, so take it away. Watch for M1 and M7: adding instead of taking away or multiplying, and dropping the word square from the unit.

content.text: A fence goes round the edge of a floor and tiles cover the inside of the same floor. Which of the two jobs needs the perimeter, and which needs the area?
content.prompt: A fence goes round the edge of a floor and tiles cover the inside of the same floor. Which of the two jobs needs the perimeter, and which needs the area?
content.publication_text: A fence goes round the edge of a floor and tiles cover the inside of the same floor. Which of the two jobs needs the perimeter, and which needs the area?

content.text:
The perimeter is the walk round the edge. The area is the amount of region inside the edge. The amount of region enclosed by a closed figure is called its area.
You met area in earlier classes on square grid paper. Count the small squares that fill a rectangle and you have its area. A rectangle that is 5 squares long and 3 squares wide holds 3 rows of 5 squares, and the count is the length multiplied by the width.
So the area of a rectangle is its length × its width. A square has the same length and width, so the area of a square is its side × its side.
Say the unit every time. The walk round the edge is in centimetres or metres. The covering inside is in square centimetres or square metres, written sq cm or sq m.

content.text: A carpet is laid on part of a floor. Do you find the floor that still shows by adding the carpet to the floor, or by taking the carpet away from the floor?
content.prompt: A carpet is laid on part of a floor. Do you find the floor that still shows by adding the carpet to the floor, or by taking the carpet away from the floor?
content.publication_text: A carpet is laid on part of a floor. Do you find the floor that still shows by adding the carpet to the floor, or by taking the carpet away from the floor?

content.text:
To find a leftover region, find the area of the whole region first. Then find the area of the part that is covered, and take it away.
Each area is found by multiplying. A rectangle is its length × its width. A square is its side × its side.
Area questions also run backwards. When the area and one side of a rectangle are known, divide the area by that side to find the other side.
When a price is given for each hundred square metres, find how many blocks of a hundred square metres fit in the plot. Then multiply by the price of one block.
A figure that is not a rectangle can be cut into rectangles. Find the area of each piece and add them.

content.text: A floor is $5\text{ m}$ long and $4\text{ m}$ wide. A square carpet of side $3\text{ m}$ is laid on the floor. Find the area of the floor that is not carpeted.
content.question: A floor is 5 m long and 4 m wide. A square carpet of side 3 m is laid on the floor. Find the area of the floor that is not carpeted.
content.book_number: Example 3: A carpet on a floor
content.question_tex: A floor is $5\text{ m}$ long and $4\text{ m}$ wide. A square carpet of side $3\text{ m}$ is laid on the floor. Find the area of the floor that is not carpeted.
content.publication_text: A floor is $5\text{ m}$ long and $4\text{ m}$ wide. A square carpet of side $3\text{ m}$ is laid on the floor. Find the area of the floor that is not carpeted.

content.text:
$1$. The area of the floor is $5\text{ m} \times 4\text{ m} = 20\text{ sq m}$.
$2$. The area of the carpet is $3\text{ m} \times 3\text{ m} = 9\text{ sq m}$.
$3$. The floor that is not carpeted is the whole floor take away the carpet: $20\text{ sq m} - 9\text{ sq m} = 11\text{ sq m}$.
Answer: $11\text{ sq m}$ is not carpeted.

The area of the carpet is 3 m × 3 m = 9 sq m.
The floor that is not carpeted is the whole floor take away the carpet: 20 sq m - 9 sq m = 11 sq m.
content.answer: 11 sq m is not carpeted.

content.question_tex: Four square flower beds, each of side $4\text{ m}$, are in the four corners of a piece of land $12\text{ m}$ long and $10\text{ m}$ wide. Find the area of the remaining part of the land.
content.publication_text: Four square flower beds, each of side $4\text{ m}$, are in the four corners of a piece of land $12\text{ m}$ long and $10\text{ m}$ wide. Find the area of the remaining part of the land.

content.text:
$1$. The area of the whole land is $12\text{ m} \times 10\text{ m} = 120\text{ sq m}$.
$2$. The area of one flower bed is $4\text{ m} \times 4\text{ m} = 16\text{ sq m}$.
$3$. The four flower beds cover $4 \times 16\text{ sq m} = 64\text{ sq m}$.
$4$. The remaining land is the whole land take away the four beds: $120\text{ sq m} - 64\text{ sq m} = 56\text{ sq m}$.
Answer: $56\text{ sq m}$ remains.

The area of one flower bed is 4 m × 4 m = 16 sq m.
The four flower beds cover 4 × 16 sq m = 64 sq m.
The remaining land is the whole land take away the four beds: 120 sq m - 64 sq m = 56 sq m.
content.answer: 56 sq m remains.

video_script.anchor: How wide is the garden?
video_script.design: One idea: when the area is known, work backwards by dividing. It assumes the child can multiply a length by a width. The wrong idea is some students's: take away instead of dividing. The anchor question stays up from the hook to the break; one clear, at the part boundary before the idea.
never_show: the width of the garden before the child has answered
the number of trees before the child has answered
video_script.wrong_move: some students takes the length of twenty-five from the area of three hundred and says two hundred seventy-five; area was made by multiplying, so it is undone by dividing, and the width is found by dividing three hundred by twenty-five.
maths_rules: The garden is a rectangle 25 m long with its width marked by a question mark and its area 300 sq m written inside.
The 300 unit squares are laid out in rows of 25 along the length, and there are 300 / 25 = 12 rows, so the width is 12 m. Check: 25 x 12 = 300 sq m.
some students's slip is 300 - 25 = 275 m, which takes the length away; area was made by multiplying, so it is undone by dividing.
The grove is 100 m long and 50 m wide, area 100 x 50 = 5000 sq m. Each tree needs 25 sq m, so the number of trees is 5000 / 25 = 200.
Forwards we multiply and backwards we divide.
video_script.payoff_line: Backwards we divide

final_answer.spoken: the garden is twelve metres wide and the grove holds two hundred trees

video_script.substitution: Area was made by multiplying, so to work backwards divide the area by the side you know or by the room one thing needs.

media.teaching_notes: Stop 1 (after the book question): How wide is the garden? Answer: 12 m. Also accept: 12, twelve, 12 m, twelve metres, 12 metres. If stuck: How many twenty-fives fit into three hundred? If wrong (275): That is a take-away. Area was made by multiplying, so to undo it we divide. Stop 2 (the hint, before the second try): How many rows of twenty-five squares fit into three hundred squares? Answer: 12 rows. Also accept: 12, twelve, twelve rows. If stuck: Count in twenty-fives: twenty-five, fifty, seventy-five, and keep going until you reach three hundred. If wrong (275): Taking away leaves squares, not rows. Count how many twenty-fives fit. Stop 3 (the second question, in the idea part): What is the area of the grove? Answer: 5000 sq m. Also accept: 5000, 5,000, five thousand, 5000 sq m, five thousand square metres. If stuck: A hundred times fifty. If wrong (300): Three hundred would be adding the sides up, which is the walk round. We want the covering inside, so multiply. Watch for M1: taking away where the question asks for a division, or adding sides where it asks for an area. Honesty note: the book asks for the maximum number of trees, and the video fills the grove so that every tree has exactly its own square metres.

video_script.anchor: How many rupees will it cost to tile the whole plot?
video_script.design: One idea: a price for every hundred square metres is charged once for each block of a hundred square metres. It assumes the child can multiply a length by a width. The wrong idea is some students's: charge for every square metre. The anchor question stays up from the hook to the break; one clear, at the part boundary before the idea.

video_script.wrong_move: some students charges eight rupees for every square metre of the plot and gets eight hundred thousand; the price is for each block of a hundred square metres, so only one thousand blocks are charged.
maths_rules: The plot is a rectangle 500 m long and 200 m wide. A price card reads 8 rupees per 100 sq m.
The area of the plot is 500 x 200 = 100000 sq m, which is 1000 blocks of 100 sq m, since 100000 / 100 = 1000.
some students's slip is 100000 x 8 = 800000 rupees, which charges 8 rupees for every square metre; the price is for every 100 sq m.
One block of 100 sq m is outlined on the plot and costs 8 rupees. The cost is 1000 x 8 = 8000 rupees.
video_script.payoff_line: Count the blocks, then price each block

video_script.substitution: Find the area of the plot, count how many blocks of a hundred square metres fit in it, and multiply by the price of one block.

media.teaching_notes: Stop 1 (after the book question): How many rupees will it cost to tile the whole plot? Answer: 8000 rupees. Also accept: 8000, 8,000, Rs 8000, eight thousand, eight thousand rupees. If stuck: First find the area of the plot, five hundred times two hundred. If wrong (800000): That charges eight rupees for every single square metre. The price is for every hundred square metres. Stop 2 (the hint, before the second try): What is the area of the plot? Answer: 100000 sq m. Also accept: 100000, 1,00,000, one lakh, 100000 sq m, a hundred thousand square metres. If stuck: Five hundred times two hundred. If wrong (700): That is the two sides added, which is a walk round. The covering inside needs multiplying. Stop 3 (the second question, in the idea part): How many blocks of one hundred square metres fit into the plot? Answer: 1000. Also accept: 1000, 1,000, a thousand, one thousand blocks. If stuck: How many hundreds are in a hundred thousand? If wrong (100): Count the zeros. A hundred thousand has five and a hundred has two, so it holds one thousand hundreds. Watch for M7: a price given for each hundred square metres is read as a price for each square metre. Honesty note: the printed solution counts one hundred thousand square metres as one thousand blocks of a hundred square metres, and the video follows it.

maths_rules: The first shape is the book's figure b, drawn to scale in metres: a top bar 5 m across and 3 m tall at the sides, with a notch cut from the bottom 3 m wide and 2 m tall. The bottom ledges are 1 m wide each.

content.text: The area of a rectangular garden $25\text{ m}$ long is $300\text{ sq m}$. What is the width of the garden?

content.publication_text: The area of a rectangular garden $25\text{ m}$ long is $300\text{ sq m}$. What is the width of the garden?

content.text:
$1$. Area $=$ length $\times$ width, so $300\text{ sq m} = 25\text{ m} \times$ width.
$2$. Going backwards, divide: width $= 300 \div 25 = 12\text{ m}$.
$3$. Check: $25\text{ m} \times 12\text{ m} = 300\text{ sq m}$.
Answer: $12\text{ m}$.

Going backwards, divide: width = 300 ÷ 25 = 12 m.
Check: 25 m × 12 m = 300 sq m.

content.text: A rectangular coconut grove is $100\text{ m}$ long and $50\text{ m}$ wide. If each coconut tree needs $25\text{ sq m}$, what is the maximum number of trees that can be planted in this grove?

content.book_number: How many coconut trees fit in the grove?

content.text:
$1$. The area of the grove is $100\text{ m} \times 50\text{ m} = 5000\text{ sq m}$.
$2$. Each tree needs $25\text{ sq m}$, so the number of trees is $5000 \div 25 = 200$.
$3$. This is the maximum because every tree uses exactly its $25\text{ sq m}$ and none of the grove is left over.
Answer: $200$ trees.

content.text: What is the cost of tiling a rectangular plot of land $500\text{ m}$ long and $200\text{ m}$ wide at the rate of $8$ rupees per hundred square metres?

content.text:
$1$. The area of the plot is $500\text{ m} \times 200\text{ m} = 100000\text{ sq m}$.
$2$. One block of $100\text{ sq m}$ costs $8$ rupees, so find how many blocks fit: $100000 \div 100 = 1000$ blocks.
$3$. The cost is $1000 \times 8 = 8000$ rupees.
Answer: Rs $8,000$, since $100,000\text{ sq m}$ is $1,000$ blocks of $100\text{ sq m}$.

video_script.design: One idea: sort the squares at the edge of a shape by how much of each is inside, and count by the four rules. It assumes the child knows a square unit. maths_rules: A curved shape is traced onto squared paper where every square is 1 unit by 1 unit, which is 1 square unit.
Rule one: a full square counts as 1 square unit. The full squares slide into a pile.
Rule two: ignore a part that is less than half a square. Rule three: a square more than half inside counts as 1 square unit.
Rule four: a square exactly half inside counts as 1/2 square unit, so two halves make 1 square unit.

media.teaching_notes: Stop 1 (after the book question): One edge square is mostly covered by the shape. Should that square be counted, or ignored? Answer: Count it, as one square unit. Also accept: count it, yes, as one, as a whole, as a whole one. If stuck: Is more than half of it inside the shape, or less? If wrong (ignore): We only ignore a square when less than half is inside. This one is mostly inside. Stop 2 (after the slip): What should we do with an edge square that has only a small part inside the shape? Answer: Ignore it. Also accept: leave it out, do not count it, skip it, ignore. If stuck: Is more than half of it inside the shape, or less? If wrong (count it as one): That would give a whole square for a small bit. Area is the covering inside, so a small part is ignored. Stop 3 (the your-turn question, at the end): A shape has 5 whole squares, 3 edge squares that are more than half inside, 2 that are less than half inside and 4 that are exactly half inside. What is its area in square units? Answer: 10 square units. Also accept: 10, ten, 10 sq units, ten square units. If stuck: Whole squares and more-than-half squares count as one each, and a square that is less than half is ignored. Four halves make how many whole squares? If wrong (14): Fourteen counts every part as a whole. The two small squares are ignored and the four halves make only two. Watch for M6: counting the squares the edge passes through instead of the squares inside. The first stop is the first rule being discovered, so give the child time. The book shows no leaf, so the video uses a curved shape traced onto squared paper.

Three panels side by side on a white background, each showing the same rectangle at the same size. Flat illustration, thin dark outlines, flat fills. Below the first two panels a shared bracket, below the third panel its own line, and a caption across the bottom of the picture. The gaps between circles are filled in the muted red of the nope colour so that they read as wasted space.

Exact mathematical structure:
- Three panels of one and the same rectangle at the same size and in the same position, with no letters or lengths on its sides.
- The first panel holds circles in straight rows and columns, with every gap between the circles filled with the nope colour, and the number 42 printed below it.

- any gap drawn between the squares in the third panel, or any square drawn overlapping another
- the gaps between circles left white instead of filled with the nope colour
- the three rectangles drawn at different sizes or the circles drawn at different sizes from panel to panel

- perimeter drawn as a filled region or area drawn as a line: the boundary is always teal on the edge, the inside is always amber

media.teaching_notes: Stop 1 (after the book question): Why are the spaces between the circles a problem when we measure an area? Answer: They leave gaps, so the rectangle is not fully covered. Also accept: gaps, spaces left, it does not fill it, bits are missed, some of it is not covered. If stuck: Is every part of the rectangle covered by a circle? If wrong (circles are round): That is true, but say what it causes. Look at the white bits between the circles. Stop 2 (after the slip): Can one rectangle have two different areas? Answer: No, one rectangle has one area. Also accept: no, it cannot, only one, the same. If stuck: The rectangle did not change size between the two packings. Did its area change? If wrong (yes): The rectangle stayed the same size, so its area stayed the same. The counts changed only because of how the circles were packed. Stop 3 (the your-turn question, at the end): A plot is to be tiled. Should the tiles be circles or squares, and why? Answer: Squares, because squares fit with no gaps and no overlaps. Also accept: squares, they fit together, no spaces left, no gaps. If stuck: Think about the white spaces you saw between the circles. If wrong (circles): Circles leave spaces between them, so part of the plot would stay bare. The counts of forty-two and forty-four are the printed ones for the same rectangle packed two ways. The video does not mention triangles, because the book only asks the child to try a triangle and a rectangle and to list the merits of the square. No misconception from the chapter list fits this video, so the slip is about which count is the true area.

content.text:
A shape with a curved or bent edge does not fit the squares exactly, so its area can only be estimated. Trace it onto squared paper where every square is 1 unit by 1 unit, which is 1 square unit.
Rule one: a full square counts as 1 square unit. Rule two: ignore a part that is less than half a square.
Rule three: if more than half of a square is inside the shape, count it as 1 square unit. Rule four: if exactly half of a square is inside, count it as half a square unit.
Count the squares inside the shape, not the squares that the edge touches. Write the answer in square units, because you counted squares.

content.text:
What are the four rules for counting squares to estimate an area on squared paper?
Answer: A full square is 1 square unit; a part more than half a square counts as 1; a part less than half is ignored; exactly half a square counts as 1/2.

content.text: The same rectangle is filled with circles, and then the circles are packed another way. Do you think both ways hold the same number of circles?

content.text:
To measure an area, we count how many units fill a region. A good unit must fill the region with no gaps and no overlaps.
Circles cannot be packed tightly. There are always gaps between them. The same rectangle was packed in two different ways with circles: one way held 42 circles and the other held 44.
A count that changes with the way you pack is not a fair measure. Squares fit edge to edge with no gaps and no overlaps, so the count is the same however you arrange them.
Squares also line up in rows and columns, so they are easy to count and easy to multiply. That makes the square the best shape to measure area.

content.text:
Draw a circle of diameter 3 on a graph sheet. Count the squares and use them to estimate the area of the circular region.
1. Draw the circle with a width of 3 squares, then count the squares that are whole inside it.
2. Look at each square on the edge. Count it as 1 if more than half of it is inside, ignore it if less than half is inside, and count it as 1/2 if exactly half is inside.
3. Add the whole squares and the edge squares that you counted. The area comes to about 7 square units.
Answer: About 7 square units, found with the half-square rule.

content.text:
Why can we not use circles instead of squares to find the area?
{{DIAGRAM:M2.S15.T15.C71.IMG2}}
1. Pack a rectangle with circles. There are gaps between the circles, so the circles do not cover the whole rectangle.
2. Pack the same rectangle in another way. The first packing holds 42 circles and the second holds 44, so one rectangle gives two different counts.
3. Squares fit edge to edge with no gaps and no overlaps, so the count of squares is the same every time.
Answer: Circles leave gaps, so the count changes with the packing; squares tile with no gaps and no overlaps.

media.teaching_notes: Stop 1 (after the book question): How many square units does the first shape cover? Answer: 4 square units. Also accept: 4, four, 4 sq units, four square units. If stuck: Count the whole squares first, then look at the edges. If wrong: Check the edge squares. Each one is cut in half, so it counts as half a square, not a whole one. Stop 2 (the hint, before the second try): Which squares are the whole squares, and which edge squares are exactly half? Answer: three whole squares and two exact halves. Also accept: 3 whole and 2 halves, three and two halves. If stuck: A whole square has all four corners inside the shape. A half square is cut corner to corner. If wrong (counts every square the edge passes through): That counts the edge and not the inside. Count only the squares that are inside the shape. Stop 3 (the second shape, in the idea part): How many square units does the second shape cover? Answer: 9 square units. Also accept: 9, nine, 9 sq units, nine square units. If stuck: Count the whole squares first, then the half squares in pairs. If wrong: Check the edge squares. Each one is cut in half, so it counts as half a square, not a whole one. Watch for M6: counting the squares the edge passes through. Counts agreed with the printed answers: the four shapes on the grid of dots hold 3 whole and 2 halves, 6 whole and 6 halves, 7 whole and 6 halves, and 8 whole and 6 halves. Every edge square of the four shapes is cut exactly in half, so the half rule decides each one.

content.text:
{{DIAGRAM:M2.S16.T16.C74.IMG1}}
$1$. The first figure has $3$ whole squares and $2$ squares that are exactly half: $3 + \frac{1}{2} + \frac{1}{2} = 4$ square units.
$2$. The second figure has $6$ whole squares and $6$ half squares: $6 + 6 \times \frac{1}{2} = 9$ square units.
$3$. The third figure has $7$ whole squares and $6$ half squares: $7 + 6 \times \frac{1}{2} = 10$ square units.
$4$. The fourth figure has $8$ whole squares and $6$ half squares: $8 + 6 \times \frac{1}{2} = 11$ square units.
Answer: $4$, $9$, $10$ and $11$ square units.

video_script.design: One idea: with the area fixed, the shape decides the perimeter. It assumes the child knows what the edge of a shape is and what area means. maths_rules: There are always twenty-four amber squares, never added to and never taken away; they only slide into new rows. The area stays 24 square units.
The perimeters are 1 x 24: 2 x (1 + 24) = 50, 2 x 12: 2 x (2 + 12) = 28, 3 x 8: 2 x (3 + 8) = 22 and 4 x 6: 2 x (4 + 6) = 20, drawn as a teal line round the edge, never as a filled region.
some students's slip is that every rectangle has a perimeter of 50; the second rectangle, 28, shows it is wrong.
For thirty-two squares: 1 x 32 gives 66, 2 x 16 gives 36 and 4 x 8 gives 24. The shortest is the one closest to a square.
your turn: eighteen squares as 1 x 18 (perimeter 38) or 3 x 6 (perimeter 18), so the long thin one has the longer walk, never shown.

final_answer.spoken: the long thin rectangle has the longest walk and the one closest to a square has the shortest
