media.teaching_notes: Stop 1 (the hook, on the two rectangles): Both rectangles cover exactly the same twenty-four squares. Do you think the walk round the edge is the same for both? Answer: no right answer, this is a prediction. Also accept: yes, no, the long one is longer, I do not know. If stuck: Just say yes or no. We are guessing. If wrong: none, a prediction cannot be wrong; say let us find out by walking both edges. Stop 2 (after the slip): The squares have been rearranged into four rows of six. What is the perimeter of this rectangle? Answer: 20 units. Also accept: 20, twenty, 20 units, twenty units. If stuck: How long is each of the four sides of the rectangle? If wrong (24): Twenty-four is the number of squares, which is the area. The perimeter is the walk round the edge. Stop 3 (the your-turn question, at the end): Eighteen squares make a rectangle of one by eighteen or one of three by six. Which has the longer walk round its edge? Answer: the 1 by 18 rectangle, 38 units against 18 units. Also accept: one by eighteen, the long one, the long thin one, 1 by 18. If stuck: Walk each edge. Add the two sides and double. If wrong (3 by 6): Both use the same eighteen squares. The long thin one has the longer walk. Folded hook: Two Fields, One Farmer opens the video in the hook part: the situation of two rectangles of one area and its one prediction question are the first stop; the fields are told as two rectangles and there is no farmer, because the book has none. Watch for M4: a child who says every rectangle of the same squares has the same walk has not tried a second rectangle. Watch for M1: a child who gives twenty-four has given the area.

interaction_points.answer: greatest 1 by 24 (50), least 4 by 6 (20); for 32: greatest 1 by 32 (66), least 4 by 8 (24)

maths_rules: There are nine unit squares, each joined to another along a whole side, in one piece with no holes. The area is always 9 square units.
The 3 x 3 block has a perimeter of 2 x (3 + 3) = 12 units. The line of nine squares has a perimeter of 2 x (9 + 1) = 20 units.

A new square always has 4 sides. If it touches 1 side it hides 1 and adds 3: 24 + 3 - 1 = 26. If it touches 2 sides it hides 2 and adds 2: 24 + 2 - 2 = 24. If it touches 3 sides it hides 3 and adds 1: 24 + 1 - 3 = 22.
some students's slip is that the perimeter goes up by 4, which adds all four sides and forgets the sides that are hidden.

media.teaching_notes: Stop 1 (the hook, on the block of nine squares): The nine squares make a three by three block with a perimeter of twelve units. If the same nine squares are spread out, does the perimeter go up or down? Answer: up, it gets bigger. Also accept: up, more, bigger, longer, increases. If stuck: Think about a straight line of nine squares. Is its walk longer or shorter than the block's? If wrong (down): Spreading the squares out leaves more of their edges on the outside. Let us walk the line and check. Stop 2 (after the slip): A new square slides into a notch where it touches two sides of the figure. Does the perimeter go up, go down or stay the same? Answer: it stays the same. Also accept: stay the same, same, no change, it does not change. If stuck: The square hides the sides it touches and adds the rest. Count both. If wrong (up): Look at the sides it covers up as it slots in. Those stop being part of the edge, so it hides two and adds two. Stop 3 (the your-turn question, at the end): A new square touches three sides of a figure that has a perimeter of thirty units. What is the new perimeter? Answer: 28 units. Also accept: 28, twenty-eight, 28 units. If stuck: Count the sides the new square hides and the sides it adds. A square has four sides. If wrong (34): That adds the square's four sides and forgets the three it hides. The new square hides what it touches. Watch for M5: a child who says the perimeter goes up by four has added all four sides of the new square and forgotten that the joined sides disappear. Honesty note: the book prints only two nine-square figures, the block with a perimeter of twelve and a C-shape with a perimeter of twenty. The line of nine squares is the video's own example; it has a perimeter of twenty as well.

content.text:
The area of a rectangle is the number of squares that cover it. Many different rectangles can be made from the same number of squares, as long as the sides are whole numbers.
Take 24 squares. Rearrange them into 1 row of 24, 2 rows of 12, 3 rows of 8 or 4 rows of 6. No square is added or taken away, so the area stays 24 square units every time.
The walk round the edge changes. The perimeter is 2 × (1 + 24) = 50 for the long row, and 2 × (4 + 6) = 20 for 4 rows of 6.
For the same area, the long thin rectangle has the greatest perimeter and the rectangle closest to a square has the least. The same pattern holds for 32 square units.

content.text:
The squares in a figure must join along whole sides, and the figure must be one piece with no holes. The area of nine squares is always 9 square units, however they are arranged.
A 3 by 3 block has a perimeter of 2 × (3 + 3) = 12. A straight line of 9 squares has a perimeter of 2 × (9 + 1) = 20. The tighter the squares are packed, the less edge is left outside.
When two squares touch, the side they share is hidden inside the figure and is no longer part of the walk. Packing the squares closely hides as many sides as possible.
Attach one new square to a figure and count the sides it hides and the sides it adds. A square on a flat side hides 1 and adds 3, so the perimeter goes up by 2. In a notch it can hide 2 and add 2, so nothing changes. In a slot it can hide 3 and add 1, so the perimeter goes down by 2.

MATHEMATICAL IMAGE REQUIREMENT
Teaching purpose: Make it obvious that every triangle drawn on the base of a rectangle, with its top corner on the opposite side, is half of that rectangle: three different-looking triangles in three rectangles of the same size all carry the same area, and the rectangle is shown once more with its own area and the half beside it.

Composition: Flat, friendly educational illustration for a middle-school maths lesson: plain white background, thin uniform dark outlines (#2B2B2B), flat fills with no shading and no gradients, clean sans-serif labels in plain classroom English a child can read aloud. Colour-blind-safe colours: teal #0072B2 for the boundary or perimeter, drawn on the boundary line, amber #E69F00 for the enclosed region or area, drawn filling the inside, green #009E73 for a correct or matched case, reddish purple #CC79A7 for the piece being asked about, grey #6B7280 for construction lines and grids, muted red #D55E00 only for a wrong or impossible case, never as decoration. 16:9 landscape, 1456 by 816 pixels. Flat illustration on a white background, thin dark outlines and flat fills. Three panels sit in a row across the upper part, each a rectangle of the same size on a faint grid. Under the three panels runs one shared caption band, and beneath it a bottom strip holds the rectangle once more. The grid is six squares long and four high in every rectangle.

Exact mathematical structure:
- Exactly three panels in a row, each a rectangle of the same size, 6 squares long and 4 squares high, drawn on a faint grey grid in the build colour.
- Panel 1: a diagonal is drawn from one corner to the opposite corner; the lower triangle is filled amber and the upper triangle is left white, and each triangle carries the label 12.
- Panel 2: a triangle with its base along the bottom side and its top corner part of the way along the top side is filled amber and labelled 12; a thin dashed drop line in the build grey runs from that corner straight down to the base, and the two smaller rectangles it makes are outlined thinly.
- Panel 3: a third triangle with its base along the bottom side and its top corner at a different point of the top side is filled amber and labelled 12.
- One shared caption band runs across all three panels under them, with the words: Different-looking triangles. Same rectangle. Same area: half of it, every time.
- The bottom strip shows the same rectangle once more with the label Area = 24 and, beneath it, the label Triangle = 12, with a large ½ sign drawn between them.

Visible text:
- 12
- Different-looking triangles. Same rectangle. Same area: half of it, every time.
- Area = 24
- Triangle = 12
- ½

Critical rejection conditions:
- any triangle whose base is not a whole side of the rectangle, or whose top corner is not on the opposite side
- the three rectangles drawn at different sizes or with different proportions
- a triangle filled in any colour but amber, or a rectangle edge in any colour but dark ink
- any muted red or green, because nothing here is wrong or matched
- the label 12 missing from any triangle, or a different number on any of them
- any text beyond the listed visible text, or any listed text misspelled or altered
- any board name, publisher name, book title, page number or curriculum branding anywhere in the frame
- a right angle drawn visibly different from 90 degrees, or sides that are shown equal but drawn visibly unequal
- perimeter drawn as a filled region or area drawn as a line: the boundary is always teal on the edge, the inside is always amber

media.teaching_notes: Stop 1 (the hook, on the two paper triangles): The paper rectangle has been cut along the diagonal and the two triangles lie side by side. Do you think they are the same size, or is one bigger? Answer: no right answer, this is a prediction. Also accept: the same, one is bigger, I do not know. If stuck: Just say what it looks like to you. If wrong: none, a prediction cannot be wrong; say let us check by putting one on top of the other. Stop 2 (after the grid, at the end of the ground part): The rectangle is six squares long and four squares high, and the diagonal cuts it in two. How many squares does one triangle cover? Answer: 12 squares. Also accept: 12, twelve, 12 squares, half of the rectangle. If stuck: The two triangles are equal, and together they cover twenty-four. If wrong (24): Twenty-four is the whole rectangle. The diagonal splits it into two triangles. Stop 3 (after the slip): The yellow triangle is as tall as the blue rectangle and its base is twice as wide. Is its area more than, less than or the same as the blue rectangle's? Answer: the same. Also accept: the same, equal, no difference, same area. If stuck: Look at the line down the middle of the yellow triangle. What two pieces does it make? If wrong (half): The yellow triangle is half of a rectangle that is twice as wide as the blue one, not half of the blue one. Stop 4 (the your-turn question, at the end): A grid rectangle is five squares long and four high, and a diagonal cuts it in two. How many squares does one triangle cover? Answer: 10 squares. Also accept: 10, ten, 10 squares, half of twenty. If stuck: Find the area of the whole rectangle first. How many equal pieces does the diagonal make? If wrong (20): Twenty is the whole rectangle. The triangle is half of it. Folded hook: One Cut, Two Pieces opens the video in the hook part: the paper rectangle, the diagonal and the cut come first, and its one prediction about the two triangles is the first stop. Watch for M8: a child who says every triangle is half of any rectangle has not matched the base and the height of the triangle. Printed-book doubt: measured on the printed figure, the yellow triangle has a base twice the width of the blue rectangle and the same height, so the two areas are the same; the answer list in the plan map says the triangle is half of the rectangle, and the video follows the figure.

content.text: A rectangle of paper is cut from one corner to the opposite corner. Do you think the two triangles are the same size, or is one bigger?

content.text:
A diagonal is a line that joins one corner of a rectangle to the opposite corner. Cut a paper rectangle along a diagonal and you get two triangles.
Lay one triangle on top of the other and turn it until the edges line up. They fit exactly, with nothing left over, so the two triangles have the same area. Try it on other rectangles, and on a square: it always works.
The two triangles together make the whole rectangle, so each one is half of it. On a grid, a rectangle 6 squares long and 4 squares high covers 6 × 4 = 24 squares, and one triangle covers 24 ÷ 2 = 12.
A triangle is half of the rectangle that fits it snugly, the one with the same base and the same height. A triangle drawn on a different base is half of a different rectangle.

content.text:
On a grid, rectangle ABCD is 5 squares wide and 4 squares high, so its area is 5 × 4 = 20 square units. The blue triangle BAD has the same base and height as the rectangle, so it is half of ABCD, which is 10 square units.
The red triangle ABE has its top corner E on the top side, part of the way along. Drop a line from E straight down to F on the bottom side. This splits ABE into triangle AEF and triangle BEF.
Triangle AEF is half of rectangle AFED, which is 3 × 4 = 12, so it is 6. Triangle BEF is half of rectangle BFEC, which is 2 × 4 = 8, so it is 4. Together they make 6 + 4 = 10, half of ABCD again.
A triangle drawn on the same base as a rectangle and between the same parallel lines is half the area of that rectangle, wherever its top corner is. To find the area of a figure with slanted sides, split it into rectangles and triangles, find each piece and add.

content.text:
- A triangle on the same base as a rectangle and between the same parallels is half of that rectangle.
- Slide the top corner along the top side and the triangle keeps the same area, because the rectangle around it does not change.
- To find the area of a figure with slanted sides, split it into rectangles and triangles, find each piece and add.

video_script.anchor: What is the area of each figure?
video_script.design: One idea: any figure with slanted sides is a set of rectangles and triangles, so split it, find each piece and add. It assumes the child knows a triangle is half of its rectangle. There is no wrong move to break here. The anchor question stays up all video; one clear, at the part boundary before the idea.
never_show: the area of any figure before the child has tried
the pieces of any figure before the hint
maths_rules: First figure: a rectangle 4 wide and 5 high is 4 x 5 = 20, with a thin triangle above (4 wide, 1 high) and one below (4 wide, 1 high), each 4 x 1 / 2 = 2. Total 20 + 2 + 2 = 24.
Second figure: a rectangle 4 wide and 5 high is 20, a triangle above 4 wide and 3 high is 4 x 3 / 2 = 6, and a triangle below 4 wide and 2 high is 4 x 2 / 2 = 4. Total 20 + 6 + 4 = 30.

Third figure: split by the line down the middle from the top corner. Left part: a rectangle 3 wide and 8 high is 24, with two small triangles of 3 x 2 / 2 = 3 each, so 30. Right part: a triangle with base 12 and height 3 is 12 x 3 / 2 = 18. Total 30 + 18 = 48.
Fourth figure: a rectangle 4 wide and 3 high is 12, with a small triangle of 1 x 2 / 2 = 1 and a triangle of 3 x 2 / 2 = 3 above it. Total 12 + 1 + 3 = 16.
Fifth figure: split across the widest part. The top triangle has base 4 and height 2, so 4 x 2 / 2 = 4. The bottom triangle has base 4 and height 4, so 4 x 4 / 2 = 8. Total 4 + 8 = 12.
The dashed cut lines and the pieces are drawn on the figures, never any area, until the idea part.

media.teaching_notes: Stop 1 (after the book question): The first figure has a slanted side at the top and a slanted side at the bottom. What shapes do you think it splits into? Answer: a rectangle and triangles, a rectangle in the middle with a triangle above and one below. Also accept: rectangle and triangle, rectangles, two triangles and a rectangle, any sensible split. If stuck: Look for a part with square corners and a part with a slanted side. If wrong: any split that uses rectangles and triangles is fine, so ask the child to say which pieces they can see; there is more than one right way to cut the figure. Stop 2 (the hint, before the second try): Cut the first figure along the grid lines into pieces you know. What is the area of the whole figure? Answer: 24 square units. Also accept: 24, twenty-four, 24 square units. If stuck: The middle rectangle is four squares wide and five high. Find that first, then the two thin triangles. If wrong (20): Twenty is only the rectangle in the middle. Add the area of the two thin triangles as well. Honesty note: the book asks for rectangles and triangles; the printed areas of 24, 30, 48, 16 and 12 square units all check on the figures, and any split that works is right.

content.text:
{{DIAGRAM:M2.S19.T19.C82.IMG1}}
$1$. The sides must multiply to $24$: $1 \times 24$, $2 \times 12$, $3 \times 8$ and $4 \times 6$.
$2$. Find each perimeter by doubling the sum of the sides: $2 \times (1 + 24) = 50$, $2 \times (2 + 12) = 28$, $2 \times (3 + 8) = 22$ and $2 \times (4 + 6) = 20$.
$3$. The greatest perimeter is $50\text{ units}$, from the long thin $1$ by $24$. The least is $20\text{ units}$, from the $4$ by $6$, which is the closest to a square.
Answer: $1$ by $24$ has a perimeter of $50\text{ units}$, $2$ by $12$ has $28$, $3$ by $8$ has $22$ and $4$ by $6$ has $20$. The greatest is the $1$ by $24$ and the least is the $4$ by $6$.

The greatest perimeter is 50 units, from the long thin 1 by 24. The least is 20 units, from the 4 by 6, which is the closest to a square.

content.publication_text:

{{DIAGRAM:M2.S19.T19.C93.IMG1}}

content.text:
{{DIAGRAM:M2.S19.T19.C94.IMG1}}
$1$. Count the sides the new square hides and the sides it adds. A square always has $4$ sides.
$2$. On a flat side it touches $1$ side: it hides $1$ and adds $3$, so the perimeter becomes $24 + 3 - 1 = 26$.
$3$. In a notch where it touches $2$ sides, it hides $2$ and adds $2$, so the perimeter stays $24 + 2 - 2 = 24$.
$4$. In a slot where it touches $3$ sides, it hides $3$ and adds $1$, so the perimeter becomes $24 + 1 - 3 = 22$.
Answer: The perimeter can go up, go down or stay the same, depending on where the square is attached.

MATHEMATICAL IMAGE REQUIREMENT
Teaching purpose: Show that every missing measurement in a house plan is forced by the rooms next to it: a clean plan with every room filled in, the places where rooms must share a measurement marked with thin lines, and the whole plot with its total area.

Composition: Flat, friendly educational illustration for a middle-school maths lesson: plain white background, thin uniform dark outlines (#2B2B2B), flat fills with no shading and no gradients, clean sans-serif labels in plain classroom English a child can read aloud. Colour-blind-safe colours: teal #0072B2 for the boundary or perimeter, drawn on the boundary line, amber #E69F00 for the enclosed region or area, drawn filling the inside, green #009E73 for a correct or matched case, reddish purple #CC79A7 for the piece being asked about, grey #6B7280 for construction lines and grids, muted red #D55E00 only for a wrong or impossible case, never as decoration. 16:9 landscape, 1456 by 816 pixels. One large floor plan fills the frame on a white background, drawn as a flat illustration with thin dark ink walls and flat fills. The plot is a rectangle wider than it is tall. The total sits in a box at the bottom right, and the two outside measurements run along the top and the right edge.

Exact mathematical structure:
- The plot is one rectangle, 35 ft wide and 30 ft tall, divided into eight rooms by ink walls; the measurement 35 ft runs along the top outside the plan and 30 ft runs down the right outside the plan.
- The left column is 15 ft wide: the master bedroom on top, the small bedroom under it, and the garden along the bottom. The garden is wider than the column: it runs 20 ft, under the small bedroom and under the toilet column.
- The toilet is a narrow room, 5 ft wide and 10 ft tall, at the top between the master bedroom and the kitchen. It is shorter than the master bedroom beside it, so a small square gap, 5 ft by 5 ft, is left under the toilet and that gap belongs to the hall.
- The right column is 15 ft wide: the utility and the kitchen at the top and the parking at the bottom. The hall fills the space between the kitchen and the parking and reaches 5 ft further left, under the toilet column, so it is 20 ft wide. The hall is an L-shape: a 20 ft by 12 ft block with the 5 ft by 5 ft square on top of its left end, under the toilet. The hall's two parts have no wall between them.
- Every room carries two lines of label: its measurements and its area, all filled in. The hall carries its two parts and one total.
- Three thin lines in the focus colour run across the plan where rooms must share a measurement, each labelled with the shared number: the height of the small bedroom and the hall, the width of the left column, and the depth of the garden and the parking.
- The total area sits in a box at the bottom right.

Visible text:
- Master Bedroom 15 × 15, 225 sq ft
- Toilet 5 × 10, 50 sq ft
- Kitchen 15 × 12, 180 sq ft
- Utility 15 × 3, 45 sq ft
- Small Bedroom 15 × 12, 180 sq ft
- Hall 20 × 12 and 5 × 5, 265 sq ft
- Garden 20 × 3, 60 sq ft
- Parking 15 × 3, 45 sq ft
- 35 ft
- 30 ft
- 12 ft
- 15 ft
- 3 ft
- Total = 1,050 sq ft

Critical rejection conditions:
- the hall drawn as a plain rectangle with no 5 ft by 5 ft square under the toilet, or labelled 240 sq ft
- the toilet drawn as tall as the master bedroom beside it, which would leave no gap
- a room label missing its dimensions or its area, or a room that is not one of the eight named rooms
- any wall that does not line up with its neighbours: the alignment lines must run straight across the plan
- any text in the frame other than the room labels, the outside measurements, the three alignment labels and the total
- any text beyond the listed visible text, or any listed text misspelled or altered
- any board name, publisher name, book title, page number or curriculum branding anywhere in the frame
- a right angle drawn visibly different from 90 degrees, or sides that are shown equal but drawn visibly unequal
- perimeter drawn as a filled region or area drawn as a line: the boundary is always teal on the edge, the inside is always amber

Student takeaway: In a plan made of rectangles, every missing measurement is forced by the rooms around it, because the walls have to line up.

video_script.anchor: What is the area of the shaded rectangle?
video_script.design: One idea: rectangles with the same height have areas that follow their widths, so one known pair unlocks the next area. It assumes the child knows that area is width times height. The wrong idea is some students's: same height means same area. The anchor question stays up from the break.
never_show: the area of the shaded rectangle before the child has answered
the answer to the your-turn question: twenty-seven square centimetres
video_script.wrong_move: some students says the two bottom rectangles have the same height, so the shaded one has the same area as its neighbour, fifteen; the heights match but the widths do not, and the shaded one is twice as wide.
maths_rules: The maze is a big rectangle cut into four: top left 13 sq cm, top right 26 sq cm, bottom left 15 sq cm and bottom right shaded with a question mark. The left column is narrower than the right column. No length is given.
The top two sit side by side, so they have the same height. Area is width × height, so 26 ÷ 13 = 2 means the right one is twice as wide.
The columns run all the way down, so the bottom right is also twice as wide as the bottom left, and the bottom two share a height.
some students's slip is the shaded area equals 15, which would need the same width; the shaded rectangle is twice as wide, so its area is 15 × 2 = 30 sq cm.
your turn: top two 7 and 21 sq cm, bottom left 9 sq cm; 21 ÷ 7 = 3, so the bottom right is 9 × 3 = 27 sq cm, never shown.
video_script.payoff_line: When the heights match, the areas follow the widths

final_answer.spoken: thirty square centimetres

video_script.substitution: Rectangles with the same height have areas in the same ratio as their widths, so a known pair of areas tells how many times wider one is than the other.

media.teaching_notes: Stop 1 (after the book question): The top two rectangles have the same height and their areas are thirteen and twenty-six square centimetres. Twenty-six is how many times thirteen? Answer: 2 times. Also accept: 2, two, twice, double, two times. If stuck: Thirteen doubled is what? If wrong (13): Thirteen is how much bigger twenty-six is. We want how many times as big. Stop 2 (after the slip): The bottom left is fifteen square centimetres and the right column is twice as wide. What is the area of the shaded rectangle? Answer: 30 sq cm. Also accept: 30, thirty, 30 sq cm, thirty square centimetres. If stuck: How does the area of a rectangle change when it is twice as wide and just as tall? If wrong (15): Same width would give fifteen. But the right column is twice as wide. Stop 3 (the your-turn question, at the end): The top two rectangles are seven and twenty-one square centimetres and the bottom left is nine. What is the area of the bottom right? Answer: 27 sq cm. Also accept: 27, twenty-seven, 27 sq cm, twenty-seven square centimetres. If stuck: Compare the two areas at the top. What do they tell you about the widths? If wrong (9): Nine is the area beside it. The shaded one is three times as wide, so it is three times as big. Watch for: a child who gives fifteen thinks the same height means the same area. The widths decide. Honesty note: the figure gives no lengths, only areas, so every step uses a shared height or a shared width.

content.text: Charan's plan has some rooms with no measurements. Do you think the missing ones can be found, or would you have to measure the real house?

content.text:
A house plan is a rectangle split into rooms. Each room is a rectangle with its own length, width and area.
A room's area is its length times its width. If you know the area and one side, divide the area by that side to find the other side.
Rooms that share a wall share that measurement. A missing number is never a guess, because the walls of neighbouring rooms have to line up.
When every room is known, the area of the whole house is the length of the plot times its width. The areas of all the rooms must add up to the same number, which checks the work.
Two houses can have the same area and still be different shapes. The walks round their edges, their perimeters, can be different.

content.text: Four rectangles are packed into one big rectangle, and only three areas are given, with no lengths. Do you think the fourth area can be found without measuring anything?

content.text:
In an area maze, rectangles fit together and share sides. Sometimes only areas are given, and sometimes a few sides.
The area of a rectangle is its width times its height. If two rectangles have the same height, the one with twice the area must be twice as wide. The areas follow the widths.
If two rectangles have the same width, the areas follow the heights in the same way.
When an area and one side are known, divide the area by the side to find the other side. When the heights in a column are known, take them away from the total height to find the last one.
Each step uses something known to unlock the next. That is how you reason your way round a maze without a ruler.

video_script.anchor: Do the two houses have the same perimeter?
video_script.design: One idea: fill a plan by dividing an area by a known side and letting the walls agree, then compare two plans of the same area by their walks round the edge. It assumes the child can find a missing side from an area. The anchor question is the second question and stays up from the idea part.
never_show: the area of Sharan's house before the idea part
the two perimeters before the child has answered the second question
maths_rules: Sharan's plot is 42 ft across and 25 ft tall. Top row: master bedroom 12 wide, toilet 5 wide, kitchen 18 wide, utility 7 wide. Bottom row: small bedroom 12 wide, hall 23 wide, entrance 7 wide.
The utility sits beside the kitchen, so it is 10 ft tall. Its area is 70 sq ft, so it is 70 ÷ 10 = 7 ft wide.

12 + 23 + 7 = 42 ft across. The master bedroom is 15 ft tall and the small bedroom 10 ft, so the plot is 15 + 10 = 25 ft tall. The kitchen row is 10 ft tall, so the hall and the entrance are 25 - 10 = 15 ft tall.
The toilet is 23 - 18 = 5 ft wide because the hall below the toilet and the kitchen is 23 ft wide, and it is 10 ft tall like the kitchen.
Areas: utility 7 × 10 = 70, hall 23 × 15 = 345, entrance 7 × 15 = 105, small bedroom 12 × 10 = 120, toilet 5 × 10 = 50. The whole house is 42 × 25 = 1050 sq ft.
Perimeters: Charan 2 × (35 + 30) = 130 ft, Sharan 2 × (42 + 25) = 134 ft. The areas are equal and the walks round the edge are not.
video_script.payoff_line: Every room is forced by its neighbours

final_answer.spoken: Sharan's house is forty-two feet by twenty-five and covers one thousand and fifty square feet

video_script.substitution: Divide a room's area by the side you know, let the neighbouring walls agree, add the rooms, then compare the two walks round the edge.

media.teaching_notes: Stop 1 (after the book question): The utility is ten feet tall and its area is seventy square feet. How wide is it? Answer: 7 ft. Also accept: 7, seven, 7 ft, seven feet. If stuck: How many tens make seventy? If wrong (60): That is a take-away. The area was made by multiplying, so we divide to undo it. Stop 2 (the hint, before the second try): Try the utility again. Its area is seventy square feet and it is ten feet tall. How wide is it? Answer: 7 ft. Also accept: 7, seven, 7 ft, seven feet. If stuck: Seventy divided by ten. If wrong (60): That takes ten away. Divide the area by the ten instead. Stop 3 (the second question, in the idea part): Both houses cover one thousand and fifty square feet. Do you think their perimeters are the same? Answer: No. Also accept: no, different, not the same, not equal. If stuck: Work out the walk round each house before you decide. If wrong (yes): Have a look at the two shapes. One is long and narrow, the other is closer to a square. Watch for M4: a child who says yes believes that the same area forces the same perimeter.

video_script.design: One idea: in a maze of joined rectangles every missing value is found by dividing an area by a known side or by taking known heights away from a total. It assumes the child can find a missing side from an area. The anchor question stays up from the hook.

maths_rules: First puzzle: a flat bar of area 10 sq cm and height 2 cm lies at the bottom, 3 cm of it sticking out on the left. A tall bar of area 10 sq cm stands on its right end. A shaded square, 3 cm wide, starts 2 cm above the flat bar and reaches the top of the tall bar.
The flat bar is 10 ÷ 2 = 5 cm long, so the tall bar is 5 - 3 = 2 cm wide and 10 ÷ 2 = 5 cm tall. The shaded square is 5 - 2 = 3 cm tall and 3 cm wide, so its area is 3 × 3 = 9 sq cm.

Second puzzle: three rectangles joined in steps, 15 cm tall in all. The middle one is 42 sq cm and 6 cm tall, so it is 42 ÷ 6 = 7 cm wide. The bottom one sticks out 5 cm more, so it is 7 + 5 = 12 cm wide and 60 ÷ 12 = 5 cm tall.
The top one is 15 - 6 - 5 = 4 cm tall and 7 - 3 = 4 cm wide, so its area is 4 × 4 = 16 sq cm.

Third puzzle: the lower bar is 18 sq cm and 5 cm wide, so it is 18 ÷ 5 = 3.6 cm tall. The tall bar stands 4 cm above it, so it is 4 + 3.6 = 7.6 cm tall. Its area is 38 sq cm, so its width is 38 ÷ 7.6 = 5 cm.

media.teaching_notes: Stop 1 (after the book question): The flat bar has an area of ten square centimetres and is two centimetres high. How long is it? Answer: 5 cm. Also accept: 5, five, 5 cm, five centimetres. If stuck: How many twos make ten? If wrong (8): That is a take-away. The area was made by multiplying, so we divide to undo it. Stop 2 (the hint, before the second try): Try the flat bar again. Its area is ten square centimetres and it is two centimetres high. How long is it? Answer: 5 cm. Also accept: 5, five, 5 cm, five centimetres. If stuck: Ten divided by two. If wrong (8): That takes two away. Divide the area by the two instead. Stop 3 (the third puzzle, in the idea part): The tall bar has an area of thirty-eight square centimetres and is seven point six centimetres tall. How wide is it? Answer: 5 cm. Also accept: 5, five, 5 cm, five centimetres. If stuck: Seven point six times what makes thirty-eight? Try a whole number. If wrong (30.4): That takes the height away. The area was made by multiplying, so divide the area by the height. Honesty note: all three puzzles were rechecked on the figures. First puzzle: the flat bar is five long, the tall bar two wide and five tall, and the shaded square three by three. Second puzzle: widths seven and twelve, heights four, six and five, and the top square four by four. Third puzzle: the lower bar is five by three point six, the tall bar is seven point six tall, so its width is five.

content.text:
{{DIAGRAM:M2.S21.T21.C99.IMG1}}
$1$. The small bedroom is $15\text{ ft}$ wide and its area is $180\text{ sq ft}$, so its other side is $180 \div 15 = 12\text{ ft}$.
$2$. The hall shares its top and bottom walls with the small bedroom, so the hall is also $12\text{ ft}$ tall. It is $5 + 15 = 20\text{ ft}$ wide, as wide as the toilet column and the kitchen column together.
$3$. The kitchen $(12\text{ ft})$ and the utility reach as far down as the master bedroom $(15\text{ ft})$, so the utility is $15 - 12 = 3\text{ ft}$ tall and $15\text{ ft}$ wide. Its area is $15 \times 3 = 45\text{ sq ft}$.
$4$. The right column is $30\text{ ft}$ tall. The utility, kitchen and hall take $3 + 12 + 12 = 27\text{ ft}$, so the parking is $30 - 27 = 3\text{ ft}$ tall and $15\text{ ft}$ wide. Its area is $15 \times 3 = 45\text{ sq ft}$.
$5$. The left column is $30\text{ ft}$ tall. The master bedroom and the small bedroom take $15 + 12 = 27\text{ ft}$, so the garden is $30 - 27 = 3\text{ ft}$ tall. It is $15 + 5 = 20\text{ ft}$ wide, so its area is $20 \times 3 = 60\text{ sq ft}$.
$6$. The hall is $20\text{ ft}$ by $12\text{ ft}$, which is $20 \times 12 = 240\text{ sq ft}$. But the toilet is only $10\text{ ft}$ tall and the bedroom beside it is $15\text{ ft}$ tall, so a gap of $5\text{ ft}$ by $5\text{ ft}$ under the toilet also belongs to the hall: $5 \times 5 = 25\text{ sq ft}$.
$7$. The hall is an $L$-shape of $240 + 25 = 265\text{ sq ft}$. The printed solution gives only $240$.
Answer: Small bedroom $15 \times 12 (180)$, utility $15 \times 3 (45)$, parking $15 \times 3 (45)$, garden $20 \times 3 (60)$, hall $20 \times 12$ plus the $5 \times 5$ strip under the toilet $= 240 + 25 = 265$ (the printed solution gives only $240$).

The hall shares its top and bottom walls with the small bedroom, so the hall is also 12 ft tall. It is 5 + 15 = 20 ft wide, as wide as the toilet column and the kitchen column together.
The kitchen (12 ft) and the utility reach as far down as the master bedroom (15 ft), so the utility is 15 - 12 = 3 ft tall and 15 ft wide. Its area is 15 × 3 = 45 sq ft.
The right column is 30 ft tall. The utility, kitchen and hall take 3 + 12 + 12 = 27 ft, so the parking is 30 - 27 = 3 ft tall and 15 ft wide. Its area is 15 × 3 = 45 sq ft.
The left column is 30 ft tall. The master bedroom and the small bedroom take 15 + 12 = 27 ft, so the garden is 30 - 27 = 3 ft tall. It is 15 + 5 = 20 ft wide, so its area is 20 × 3 = 60 sq ft.

The hall is 20 ft by 12 ft, which is 20 × 12 = 240 sq ft. But the toilet is only 10 ft tall and the bedroom beside it is 15 ft tall, so a gap of 5 ft by 5 ft under the toilet also belongs to the hall: 5 × 5 = 25 sq ft.
The hall is an L-shape of 240 + 25 = 265 sq ft. The printed solution gives only 240.
content.answer: Small bedroom 15 × 12 (180), utility 15 × 3 (45), parking 15 × 3 (45), garden 20 × 3 (60), hall 20 × 12 plus the 5 × 5 strip under the toilet = 240 + 25 = 265 (the printed solution gives only 240).

content.text:
{{DIAGRAM:M2.S21.T21.C101.IMG1}}
$1$. The utility is beside the kitchen, so it is $10\text{ ft}$ tall. Its area is $70\text{ sq ft}$, so its width is $70 \div 10 = 7\text{ ft}$.
$2$. Across the bottom, the small bedroom is $12\text{ ft}$ wide and the hall is $23\text{ ft}$ wide, and $12 + 23 + 7 = 42\text{ ft}$, the width of the plot.
$3$. The master bedroom is $15\text{ ft}$ tall and the small bedroom is $10\text{ ft}$ tall, so the plot is $15 + 10 = 25\text{ ft}$ tall.
$4$. The kitchen row is $10\text{ ft}$ tall, so the hall and the entrance are $25 - 10 = 15\text{ ft}$ tall. The entrance is $7\text{ ft}$ wide, like the utility.
$5$. The hall is $23\text{ ft}$ wide and sits below the toilet and the kitchen. The kitchen is $18\text{ ft}$ wide, so the toilet is $23 - 18 = 5\text{ ft}$ wide. It is $10\text{ ft}$ tall, like the kitchen.
$6$. The areas are: utility $7 \times 10 = 70\text{ sq ft}$, hall $23 \times 15 = 345\text{ sq ft}$, entrance $7 \times 15 = 105\text{ sq ft}$, small bedroom $12 \times 10 = 120\text{ sq ft}$ and toilet $5 \times 10 = 50\text{ sq ft}$.
Answer: Utility $7 \times 10 (70)$, hall $23 \times 15 (345)$, entrance $7 \times 15 (105)$, small bedroom $12 \times 10 (120)$, toilet $5 \times 10 (50)$.
steps: The utility is beside the kitchen, so it is 10 ft tall. Its area is 70 sq ft, so its width is 70 ÷ 10 = 7 ft.
Across the bottom, the small bedroom is 12 ft wide and the hall is 23 ft wide, and 12 + 23 + 7 = 42 ft, the width of the plot.
The master bedroom is 15 ft tall and the small bedroom is 10 ft tall, so the plot is 15 + 10 = 25 ft tall.
The kitchen row is 10 ft tall, so the hall and the entrance are 25 - 10 = 15 ft tall. The entrance is 7 ft wide, like the utility.
The hall is 23 ft wide and sits below the toilet and the kitchen. The kitchen is 18 ft wide, so the toilet is 23 - 18 = 5 ft wide. It is 10 ft tall, like the kitchen.
The areas are: utility 7 × 10 = 70 sq ft, hall 23 × 15 = 345 sq ft, entrance 7 × 15 = 105 sq ft, small bedroom 12 × 10 = 120 sq ft and toilet 5 × 10 = 50 sq ft.
content.answer: Utility 7 × 10 (70), hall 23 × 15 (345), entrance 7 × 15 (105), small bedroom 12 × 10 (120), toilet 5 × 10 (50).

$1$. Both houses cover $1050\text{ sq ft}$, so their areas are equal.

content.text:
$1$. The top two rectangles have the same height. $26 \div 13 = 2$, so the top right one is twice as wide as the top left one.
$2$. The right column is twice as wide as the left column all the way down, and the bottom two rectangles share a height.
$3$. The bottom left is $15\text{ sq cm}$, so the bottom right is $15 \times 2 = 30\text{ sq cm}$.
Answer: $30\text{ sq cm}$.
steps: The top two rectangles have the same height. 26 ÷ 13 = 2, so the top right one is twice as wide as the top left one.
The right column is twice as wide as the left column all the way down, and the bottom two rectangles share a height.
The bottom left is 15 sq cm, so the bottom right is 15 × 2 = 30 sq cm.

content.text:
$1$. Second maze: the flat bar is $10\text{ sq cm}$ and $2\text{ cm}$ high, so it is $10 \div 2 = 5\text{ cm}$ long. It sticks out $3\text{ cm}$ on the left, so the tall bar is $5 - 3 = 2\text{ cm}$ wide. The tall bar is $10\text{ sq cm}$, so it is $10 \div 2 = 5\text{ cm}$ tall. The shaded square starts $2\text{ cm}$ above the flat bar, so it is $5 - 2 = 3\text{ cm}$ tall and $3\text{ cm}$ wide, and its area is $3 \times 3 = 9\text{ sq cm}$.
$2$. Third maze: the middle rectangle is $42\text{ sq cm}$ and $6\text{ cm}$ tall, so it is $42 \div 6 = 7\text{ cm}$ wide. The bottom one sticks out $5\text{ cm}$ more, so it is $7 + 5 = 12\text{ cm}$ wide, and it is $60 \div 12 = 5\text{ cm}$ tall. The heights add to $15\text{ cm}$, so the top one is $15 - 6 - 5 = 4\text{ cm}$ tall. It is $3\text{ cm}$ narrower than the middle one, so it is $7 - 3 = 4\text{ cm}$ wide and its area is $4 \times 4 = 16\text{ sq cm}$.
$3$. Fourth maze: the lower bar is $18\text{ sq cm}$ and $5\text{ cm}$ wide, so it is $18 \div 5 = 3.6\text{ cm}$ tall. The tall bar stands $4\text{ cm}$ above it, so it is $4 + 3.6 = 7.6\text{ cm}$ tall. Its area is $38\text{ sq cm}$, so its width is $38 \div 7.6 = 5\text{ cm}$.
Answer: $9\text{ sq cm}$, $16\text{ sq cm}$ and $5\text{ cm}$.

video_script.anchor: What area is asked for?
video_script.design: One idea: every area question here is solved by finding the areas by multiplying, then adding, taking away or dividing. It assumes the child can find the area of a rectangle. The anchor question is whichever area is asked for and stays up from the hook.

maths_rules: First question: two rectangles, 5 m by 10 m and 2 m by 7 m. Their areas are 5 × 10 = 50 sq m and 2 × 7 = 14 sq m. A new rectangle has the sum, 50 + 14 = 64 sq m. Any sides that multiply to 64 work: 16 × 4 = 64, 32 × 2 = 64, 8 × 8 = 64.
Second question: a garden 50 m long with area 1000 sq m. Its width is 1000 ÷ 50 = 20 m. The check is 50 × 20 = 1000 sq m.
Third question: a floor 5 m by 4 m has area 5 × 4 = 20 sq m. A square carpet of side 3 m has area 3 × 3 = 9 sq m. The floor not carpeted is 20 - 9 = 11 sq m.

final_answer.value: 64 sq m, 20 m and 11 sq m
final_answer.spoken: sixty-four square metres, twenty metres and eleven square metres

video_script.substitution: Find each area by multiplying, add or take them away as the question asks, and divide an area by a side to find the other side.

media.teaching_notes: Stop 1 (after the book question): A new rectangle must have an area equal to the two given areas added together. The two rectangles are five metres by ten metres and two metres by seven metres. What area must the new rectangle have? Answer: 64 sq m. Also accept: 64, sixty-four, 64 sq m, sixty-four square metres. If stuck: Find the area of each rectangle first. If wrong (24): That adds up the sides. We need the areas, which are made by multiplying. Stop 2 (the hint, before the second try): What are the two areas, and what do they add up to? Answer: 50 and 14, which add up to 64 sq m. Also accept: 50 and 14, fifty and fourteen, 64, sixty-four. If stuck: Five times ten, then two times seven. If wrong (17): That adds the sides again. Multiply to get each area. Stop 3 (the garden, in the idea part): A rectangular garden is fifty metres long and its area is one thousand square metres. How wide is it? Answer: 20 m. Also accept: 20, twenty, 20 m, twenty metres. If stuck: How many fifties make one thousand? If wrong (950): That is a take-away. The area was made by multiplying, so we divide to undo it. Stop 4 (the carpet, in the idea part): A floor is five metres by four metres and a square carpet with sides of three metres lies on it. How much of the floor is not carpeted? Answer: 11 sq m. Also accept: 11, eleven, 11 sq m, eleven square metres. If stuck: Find the area of the whole floor and the area of the carpet. If wrong (9): Nine is the carpet. We want the part of the floor with no carpet. Honesty note: the first question has no single answer: any rectangle of area sixty-four works, and sixteen by four, thirty-two by two and eight by eight are three of them. The printed solution of the garden question is in metres throughout; the width is twenty metres.

interaction_points.answer: 64 sq m, 20 m and 11 sq m

content.text:
These questions use the whole chapter. The area of a rectangle is its length times its width, a missing side is an area divided by the side you know, and a perimeter is the walk round the edge.
To find what is left of an area, take the part that is covered or dug out away from the whole.
Two shapes can have the same area and different perimeters. A long thin shape has a long edge even when it covers little, so a smaller area can have the longer perimeter.
When a shape is cut in two, the cut edge is walked twice, once on each piece. That is why the two perimeters added are bigger than the perimeter of the first shape.
Some questions have no single answer. Any shape that fits the conditions will do, and a border on your own page depends on your own page.

content.text:
Give the dimensions of a rectangle whose area is the sum of the areas of two rectangles measuring 5 m × 10 m and 2 m × 7 m.
1. The two areas are 5 × 10 = 50 sq m and 2 × 7 = 14 sq m.
2. The new rectangle has an area of 50 + 14 = 64 sq m.
3. Any sides that multiply to 64 work: 16 × 4 = 64, 32 × 2 = 64 and 8 × 8 = 64.
Answer: 64 sq m in all: for example 16 × 4, 32 × 2 or 8 × 8.

On a page of your book, draw a rectangular border that is 1 cm from the top and the bottom and 1.5 cm from the left and right sides. What is the perimeter of the border?
1. Measure your own page: its height and its width in centimetres.
2. The border is 1 + 1 = 2 cm shorter than the page, and 1.5 + 1.5 = 3 cm narrower.
3. The perimeter of the border is two times the sum of its height and its width.
4. Every page is different, so there is no single answer.
Answer: Depends on the page: measure it, then use 2 × (length + breadth).

content.text:
The perimeter is the walk round the edge of a shape, measured in centimetres. The area is the covering inside, measured in square centimetres.
The perimeter of a polygon is the sum of the lengths of all its sides. For a rectangle it is two times the sum of its length and width, and for a square it is four times a side.
The area of a rectangle is its length times its width. The area of a square is a side times itself.
Two shapes can have the same area with different perimeters, or the same perimeter with different areas.
The area of any shape can be found by breaking it into unit squares, or into rectangles and triangles whose areas you can find.

$1$. The garden is $15 \times 12 = 180\text{ sq m}$.
$2$. One bed is $2 \times 1 = 2\text{ sq m}$, and four beds are $4 \times 2 = 8\text{ sq m}$.
$3$. The lawn is $180 - 8 = 172\text{ sq m}$.
Answer: $172\text{ sq m}$.

content.text: A square piece of paper is folded in half. The square is then cut into two rectangles along the fold. Regardless of the size of the square, one statement is always true. Which one?
content.question: A square piece of paper is folded in half. The square is then cut into two rectangles along the fold. Regardless of the size of the square, one statement is always true. Which one?
content.book_number: Pulling It Together, Q3
content.question_tex: A square piece of paper is folded in half. The square is then cut into two rectangles along the fold. Regardless of the size of the square, one statement is always true. Which one?
content.publication_text: A square piece of paper is folded in half. The square is then cut into two rectangles along the fold. Regardless of the size of the square, one statement is always true. Which one?

content.text:
$1$. Take a square with sides of $10\text{ units}$. Its perimeter is $4 \times 10 = 40\text{ units}$.
$2$. Each rectangle is $10$ by $5$, so its perimeter is $10 + 5 + 10 + 5 = 30\text{ units}$. The two together have $30 + 30 = 60\text{ units}$.
$3$. $60 \div 40 = 1.5$, so the two perimeters added are one and a half times the square's perimeter.
$4$. It works for any side: the cut adds two new edges, each as long as a side. The two rectangles walk $4 + 2 = 6$ sides against the square's $4$, and six is one and a half times four.
$5$. The two rectangles cover exactly the square, so their areas add up to the square's area. The statements about the areas are false, and the square's perimeter is smaller than the two added.
Answer: The perimeters of the two rectangles added are always $1 \frac{1}{2}$ times the perimeter of the square.

objectives.strand_name: Perimeter: the walk round the edge
objectives.objective_text: Explain that the perimeter of a closed shape is the distance all the way round its boundary, and tell the walk along the edge apart from the covering inside.

objectives.strand_name: Perimeter: the walk round the edge
objectives.objective_text: Find the perimeter of a rectangle by adding all four sides, and explain why the rule doubles the sum of the length and the breadth.

objectives.strand_name: Perimeter: the walk round the edge
objectives.objective_text: Find the perimeter of a square as four times a side and of a triangle by adding its three sides, and find the distance for several rounds by multiplying one round.

objectives.objective_text: Find a missing side of a rectangle, a square or a triangle when its perimeter is given, by taking away the sides that are given and sharing what is left.

objectives.strand_name: Perimeter: the walk round the edge
objectives.objective_text: Find the side of each regular shape made from one wire by sharing its length equally, and find the cost of a fence and the rope for several rounds from the perimeter.

objectives.strand_name: Perimeter: the walk round the edge
objectives.objective_text: Share one length of wire equally between the sides of a regular shape, and explain why a wire of 22 centimetres cannot make a regular pentagon with whole-centimetre sides.

objectives.strand_name: Perimeter: the walk round the edge
objectives.objective_text: Find how far a runner goes in several rounds of a rectangular track by working out one round first and multiplying by the number of rounds, then compare two runners fairly.

objectives.strand_name: Perimeter: the walk round the edge
objectives.objective_text: Find where a runner is after a given distance by taking away whole rounds first, then measuring the leftover from the start, and say how many full rounds are done.

objectives.strand_name: Perimeter: the walk round the edge
objectives.objective_text: Find the distance for several rounds of a track, and place a runner after any distance by taking away whole rounds, then use the same idea to find a start point for a race.

objectives.strand_name: Perimeter: the walk round the edge
objectives.objective_text: Explain why a slanted unit on a dot grid is longer than a straight unit, and write the perimeter of a dot grid shape as straight units plus diagonal units, counted in two separate piles.

objectives.strand_name: Perimeter: the walk round the edge
objectives.objective_text: Write the perimeter of an equilateral triangle as three times a side, explain what a square and an equilateral triangle share, and write the perimeter of any regular polygon as the number of sides times one side.

objectives.strand_name: Perimeter: the walk round the edge
objectives.objective_text: Draw closed shapes on a dot grid and write each perimeter in straight and diagonal units, and decide why a closed shape cannot have exactly one straight edge with every other edge slanted.

objectives.strand_name: Perimeter: the walk round the edge
objectives.objective_text: Find the perimeter of a shape made by joining two pieces by adding the two perimeters and taking away twice the join, and explain why the joined edges stop being boundary.

objectives.strand_name: Perimeter: the walk round the edge
objectives.objective_text: Build shapes from the two pieces of a cut chit, find each perimeter from the join, and show that the paper stays the same while the edge changes.
Explain that area is the amount of region inside a closed figure counted in squares, and write the area of a rectangle and of a square in square units.
Find the area of a region left over by working out the whole area and taking away the covered part, and find a missing side or a count from a given area.
Find the area of a floor by counting its squares, find the part left showing after a carpet or flower beds are laid, and compare two floors of the same area.
Count the area of a shape drawn on squared paper using the four rules for whole, more than half, less than half and exactly half squares, and give the answer in square units.
Explain why area is measured with squares and not circles, and list the reasons that make the square the best unit, using the gaps that circles leave.
Count the area of a figure on a grid by sorting its squares into whole, more than half, less than half and exactly half, and show that circles packed two ways give different counts.
List every rectangle with whole-number sides that has a given area, find the perimeter of each, and decide which has the greatest perimeter and which has the least.
Arrange nine unit squares into connected figures, find the smallest and largest perimeter, make a perimeter of 18, and show how one added square changes a perimeter.
Arrange nine unit squares to find the smallest and largest perimeter, make a perimeter of 18, and add a tenth square to raise, lower or keep a perimeter of 24.
Explain why a diagonal cuts a rectangle into two triangles of equal area, and find the area of one triangle as half of the rectangle that fits it snugly.
Find the area of a triangle on a grid as half of the rectangle around it, write the rule in your own words, and find the area of a figure by splitting it into rectangles and triangles.
Find the area of triangles and figures on a grid by halving the rectangle around a triangle, and decide whether a triangle can ever have a different share of its rectangle.
Find every missing side and area in a house plan made of rectangles by dividing an area by a given side, then add the rooms to find the area of the whole house.
Find the missing area or side in a maze of joined rectangles, and explain how a shared side lets one given area unlock the next.
Fill in the missing sides and areas of two house plans and four area mazes by letting neighbouring rooms agree, then compare the two houses by area and perimeter.
Solve the final area and perimeter questions by adding, taking away and dividing areas, and explain why equal or smaller areas can still have longer perimeters.
Explain in your own words how perimeter and area differ, and give one example of two shapes with the same area but different perimeters.

tool_wire_bender.title: Wire Bender
tool_wire_bender.predict: Before you bend the wire, guess: when it is straightened again, will it be shorter, longer or the same?
tool_wire_bender.one_idea: The wire's length never changes, so every shape bent from it has the same perimeter, and only the way the length is shared between the sides changes.
tool_wire_bender.invariant: The wire is never cut, so its length never changes and every shape made from it has the same perimeter.

tool_grid_counter.title: Grid Counter
tool_grid_counter.predict: Before you tap a square, guess the area of the figure in square units.
tool_grid_counter.one_idea: The area of an awkward shape is found by sorting its squares into whole, more than half, less than half and exactly half.
tool_grid_counter.invariant: Only the squares inside the figure are counted, and each edge square is sorted by how much of it is inside.

tool_nine_squares.title: Nine Squares
tool_nine_squares.predict: Before you place a square, guess whether a tight block or a spread-out line will give the longer edge.
tool_nine_squares.one_idea: The same nine squares can make many shapes, and the tighter you pack them, the shorter the edge.
tool_nine_squares.invariant: The area is always 9 square units, and only the arrangement changes the perimeter.

tool_room_planner.title: Room Planner
tool_room_planner.predict: Before you fill in any room, guess which blank you can work out first.
tool_room_planner.one_idea: In a plan made of rectangles, every missing number is forced by the rooms around it, so you can reason it out instead of measuring.
tool_room_planner.invariant: Rooms that share a wall share that measurement, so every missing number is forced by its neighbours.

tool_track_runner.title: Track Runner
tool_track_runner.predict: Before you drag the dial, guess where the runner will be when the distance reaches one and a half rounds.
tool_track_runner.one_idea: Running a distance on a loop is whole rounds plus a leftover, and the leftover tells you where you are standing.
tool_track_runner.invariant: The distance run is always whole rounds plus a leftover, and the leftover is less than one round.

tool_boundary_walk.title: Boundary Walk
tool_boundary_walk.predict: Before you tap any side, guess the total walk for the shape in front of you.
tool_boundary_walk.one_idea: The perimeter is the total of the sides you walk along, and you only ever count each side once.
tool_boundary_walk.invariant: Each side is walked once, so the perimeter is the total of the sides and nothing else.

tool_floor_coverer.title: Floor Coverer
tool_floor_coverer.predict: Before you lay the carpet, guess how many squares of floor will still show.
tool_floor_coverer.one_idea: Area is how many unit squares fit inside, and a covered part is taken away from the whole.
tool_floor_coverer.invariant: The area left over is always the whole area take away the covered area.

tool_edge_or_inside.title: Edge or Inside
tool_edge_or_inside.predict: Before you switch anything on, guess: will the teal walk ever go inside the rectangle?
tool_edge_or_inside.one_idea: A shape has an edge you can walk along and an inside you can fill, and these are two different things to look at.
tool_edge_or_inside.invariant: The teal walk always stays on the edge and the amber squares always stay inside.

tool_dot_grid_builder.title: Dot Grid Builder
tool_dot_grid_builder.predict: Before you draw, guess whether a shape made only of slanted edges has a longer or a shorter edge than a shape of the same number of straight edges.
tool_dot_grid_builder.one_idea: On a dot grid, straight edges and slanted edges are different lengths, so a perimeter is counted as two separate tallies.
tool_dot_grid_builder.invariant: Every edge is either a straight unit or a diagonal unit, and a diagonal unit is always longer.

tool_split_and_rejoin.title: Split and Rejoin
tool_split_and_rejoin.predict: Before you move a piece, guess whether a longer join will make the perimeter bigger or smaller.
tool_split_and_rejoin.one_idea: Joining two pieces hides two copies of the join from the boundary, so a longer join means a shorter perimeter while the paper stays exactly the same.
tool_split_and_rejoin.invariant: The paper is always the same two pieces, so the paper readout never changes, while the perimeter changes with the join.

tool_half_the_rectangle.title: Half the Rectangle
tool_half_the_rectangle.predict: Before you slide the corner, guess whether the triangle's area will grow, shrink or stay the same.
tool_half_the_rectangle.one_idea: Every triangle on a grid is half of the rectangle drawn snugly around it.
tool_half_the_rectangle.invariant: The triangle's area is always half of the area of the snug rectangle around it.

misconceptions.fix: Ask what is being measured: the walk round the edge (centimetres) or the covering inside (square centimetres). Adding belongs to the walk, multiplying to the covering.
misconceptions.text: Mixing up perimeter and area: adding when you should multiply, or the reverse.

misconceptions.fix: Walk the whole boundary with a finger. A rectangle has two lengths and two breadths, so the walk is four sides.
misconceptions.text: For a rectangle, adding only length and breadth and forgetting the other two sides.

misconceptions.fix: Lay one straight unit along one slanted unit and watch it fall short. They stay in separate piles.
misconceptions.text: Thinking a slanted unit is the same length as a straight unit.

misconceptions.fix: Build two shapes from the same squares and walk both boundaries. The covering holds still while the walk changes.
misconceptions.text: Believing the same area forces the same perimeter.

misconceptions.fix: Trace the outside with a finger. The edges where the pieces touch are never walked, so take the join away twice.
misconceptions.text: Adding both perimeters when shapes are joined and forgetting that the join disappears.

misconceptions.fix: Area is the covering inside. Count the squares that fill the shape, not the squares the edge passes through.
misconceptions.text: Counting the boundary squares instead of the squares inside.

misconceptions.fix: The walk is in centimetres. The covering is in square centimetres. Say which one you found.
misconceptions.text: Forgetting the units, or writing cm where square cm belongs.

misconceptions.fix: Draw the rectangle that has the same base and the same height as the triangle. The triangle is half of that one.
misconceptions.text: Thinking a triangle's area is half of any rectangle instead of half of the rectangle that fits it snugly.

solution_notes.correct: On the figure the yellow triangle has the same height as the blue rectangle and a base twice as wide, so the two areas are the same: the line down the middle splits the triangle into two halves, each the size of the rectangle's own half. Teach it as 'the same area', and the later rule: a triangle is half of the rectangle with the same base and height.
solution_notes.printed_solution: The book prints no answer for the blue rectangle and the yellow triangle; the Flow says the triangle is half the rectangle.

solution_notes.correct: On the figure ABCD is 5 squares wide and 4 high with E three squares along from A: BAD is 10, AFED is 12, BFEC is 8, AEF is 6 and BEF is 4.
solution_notes.printed_solution: The Flow draws rectangle ABCD as 6 by 4.

solution_notes.correct: A new square must share a whole side. On a flat side the perimeter rises by 2, in a notch of two sides it stays the same, in a slot of three sides it falls by 2; all three outcomes are possible.
solution_notes.printed_solution: The Flow says placing the new square at a corner raises the perimeter by 2.
